organisms.name: Staphylococcus aureus
organisms.tagline: Catalase- and coagulase-positive pathogen behind skin infection, bacteraemia, endocarditis and toxin-mediated disease.
diseases: Skin and soft tissue infection (abscess, cellulitis, impetigo)

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive cocci in clusters; facultative anaerobe, non-motile, non-spore-forming.
• Catalase-positive and coagulase-positive (separates it from coagulase-negative staphylococci); ferments mannitol; beta-haemolytic on blood agar.
• MRSA carries mecA (or mecC), encoding PBP2a, which has low affinity for beta-lactams.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG and impairs opsonisation.
• Coagulase and clumping factor promote clot formation and adherence.
• Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL) is linked to necrotising skin and lung infection.
• Superantigens (TSST-1, enterotoxins) cause toxic shock and food poisoning; exfoliative toxins cause scalded skin syndrome.
• Biofilm formation on prosthetic material and catheters.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text: Roughly 20-30% of people carry S. aureus in the anterior nares. Spread is mainly by direct contact, often from the patient's own colonised sites. Risk factors include injection drug use, indwelling devices, dialysis, diabetes, surgery and recent hospitalisation. Community-associated MRSA is a frequent cause of skin abscesses.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Blood cultures (at least 2 sets) for suspected bacteraemia; repeat every 24-48 h until clear.
• Pus or abscess fluid for Gram stain and culture.
• Rapid PCR (mecA/nuc) identifies MRSA quickly.
• S. aureus in blood is never a contaminant: search for the source and consider echocardiography.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• MSSA bacteraemia: an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam (cefazolin, or flucloxacillin, nafcillin or oxacillin) is first-line. Vancomycin is inferior for MSSA.
• MRSA bacteraemia: vancomycin (AUC-guided dosing) or daptomycin.
• Uncomplicated bacteraemia: at least 14 days from the first negative culture. Endocarditis, osteomyelitis and metastatic foci need 4-6 weeks or longer.
• Source control (drain abscesses, remove infected devices) is essential.
• Mild MRSA skin infection: incision and drainage; add TMP-SMX or doxycycline when antibiotics are indicated.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text: Hand hygiene, contact precautions for MRSA, device-care bundles, and decolonisation (intranasal mupirocin with chlorhexidine bathing) in selected patients before surgery.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Skin: painful abscess or boil, impetigo, folliculitis, cellulitis.
• Bacteraemia with metastatic seeding to bone, joints, lungs and heart valves.
• Right-sided endocarditis in injection drug users; left-sided disease destroys valves quickly.
• Enterotoxin food poisoning: vomiting within 1 to 6 hours of eating, resolves in a day.
• Toxic shock: fever, rash, hypotension and multi-organ involvement.
• Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome in infants and young children.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• mecA (or mecC) encodes PBP2a, giving resistance to nearly all beta-lactams except newer anti-MRSA cephalosporins.
• Penicillinase (blaZ) makes most isolates penicillin-resistant.
• VISA from a thickened cell wall; VRSA via vanA acquired from enterococci (rare).
• Inducible clindamycin resistance (erm): detect with the D-test.

pearls: S. aureus bacteraemia carries high mortality; early source control and infectious diseases input improve outcomes.
For MSSA, beta-lactams outperform vancomycin; do not default to vancomycin once susceptibility is known.
Document clearance with repeat blood cultures.
references: Liu C et al. IDSA clinical practice guidelines for MRSA infections in adults and children. Clin Infect Dis 2011;52:e18-e55.
Tong SYC et al. Staphylococcus aureus infections: epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, and management. Clin Microbiol Rev 2015;28:603-661.
Holland TL et al. Clinical management of Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia: a review. JAMA 2014;312:1330-1341.

organisms.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
organisms.tagline: Encapsulated, alpha-haemolytic pathogen; leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia and adult bacterial meningitis.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci; alpha-haemolytic on blood agar.
• Catalase-negative, optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble.
• Polysaccharide capsule (more than 100 serotypes) is the main virulence factor; the Quellung reaction shows capsule swelling.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Capsule inhibits phagocytosis.
• Pneumolysin damages host cells and impairs immune function.
• IgA protease aids mucosal colonisation; autolysin (LytA) releases inflammatory cell-wall fragments.
• Surface proteins (PspA, choline-binding proteins) aid adhesion and complement evasion.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text: Colonises the nasopharynx, especially in children, and spreads by respiratory droplets. Highest risk: children under 2 years, adults 65 and older, asplenia or hyposplenism, sickle cell disease, immunodeficiency, chronic heart, lung, liver or kidney disease, cochlear implants and CSF leak. Conjugate vaccines have shifted the circulating serotypes.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Blood cultures and sputum Gram stain and culture.
• Urinary pneumococcal antigen supports the diagnosis of pneumonia in adults.
• CSF Gram stain, culture and PCR when meningitis is suspected.
• Penicillin susceptibility breakpoints differ for meningitis and non-meningitis isolates.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Outpatient CAP in healthy adults: amoxicillin or doxycycline; a macrolide only where local pneumococcal macrolide resistance is below 25%.
• Hospitalised CAP (non-severe): beta-lactam plus macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone.
• Meningitis: ceftriaxone plus vancomycin empirically, narrowed to susceptibility; give dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose in adults.
• Macrolide resistance is widespread, so macrolide monotherapy is unreliable.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text: Pneumococcal conjugate and polysaccharide vaccines per national schedules. Vaccinate patients with asplenia, and before splenectomy or cochlear implantation.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Lobar pneumonia: abrupt fever and rigors, productive cough with rust-coloured sputum, pleuritic chest pain, lobar consolidation.
• Meningitis: the leading cause of adult bacterial meningitis; headache, neck stiffness and altered mental state, with a risk of hearing loss.
• Otitis media and sinusitis, especially in children.
• Bacteraemia and sepsis; overwhelming post-splenectomy infection in asplenia and sickle cell disease.
• Complications: parapneumonic effusion, empyema, pericarditis.
• Risk groups: extremes of age, asplenia, alcohol use disorder, COPD, HIV, CSF leak, immunoglobulin or complement deficiency.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Penicillin resistance results from altered penicillin-binding proteins, not beta-lactamase.
• Susceptibility breakpoints differ for meningitis and non-meningitis infection; pneumonia is often still treatable with high-dose penicillin or amoxicillin.
• Macrolide resistance by erm (target modification) and mef (efflux) is common, so avoid macrolide monotherapy where local rates are high.
• Fluoroquinolone resistance through gyrA and parC mutations is uncommon.
• Empirical meningitis therapy includes vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin because of resistant strains.
• Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines have shifted circulating serotypes (serotype replacement).

pearls: Alpha-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble: the classic laboratory triad.
Most common cause of both community-acquired pneumonia and adult bacterial meningitis.
Asplenic patients can progress to fulminant sepsis within hours; treat fever as an emergency.
references: Metlay JP et al. Diagnosis and treatment of adults with community-acquired pneumonia. ATS/IDSA guideline. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200:e45-e67.
van de Beek D et al. ESCMID guideline: diagnosis and treatment of acute bacterial meningitis. Clin Microbiol Infect 2016;22(Suppl 3):S37-S62.
Weiser JN, Ferreira DM, Paton JC. Streptococcus pneumoniae: transmission, colonization and invasion. Nat Rev Microbiol 2018;16:355-367.

organisms.name: Escherichia coli
organisms.tagline: Gut commensal and the most common cause of urinary tract infection and Gram-negative bacteraemia.
diseases: Haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome (STEC)

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative bacilli, facultative anaerobe, motile.
• Lactose fermenter: pink colonies on MacConkey agar, green metallic sheen on EMB agar.
• Indole-positive and oxidase-negative.
• Pathotypes: ExPEC (UPEC, neonatal meningitis), ETEC, EPEC, EHEC/STEC, EIEC and EAEC.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• P fimbriae and type 1 fimbriae mediate urinary tract adhesion.
• K1 capsule is linked to neonatal meningitis.
• LPS endotoxin drives septic shock.
• Shiga toxin (EHEC O157:H7) causes haemorrhagic colitis and HUS; heat-labile and heat-stable toxins (ETEC) cause watery diarrhoea.
• Siderophores for iron acquisition.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text: Part of normal gut flora. Diarrhoeal pathotypes spread by the faecal-oral route through contaminated food or water. ESBL-producing and carbapenem-resistant strains are rising worldwide, particularly in healthcare settings.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Urine culture (100,000 CFU/mL is the classic threshold; lower counts can be significant in symptomatic patients).
• Blood cultures for sepsis.
• Test stool for Shiga toxin or stx genes when STEC is suspected; do not rely on O157 culture alone.
• Request ESBL and carbapenemase testing per local policy.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Uncomplicated cystitis: nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin or TMP-SMX where local resistance is low; avoid fluoroquinolones as first-line.
• Pyelonephritis and bacteraemia: ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone guided by susceptibility; step down to oral therapy once improving.
• ESBL-producing isolates: a carbapenem for serious infection outside the urinary tract; oral TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin step-down is accepted when susceptible.
• Carbapenem-resistant isolates: treatment depends on the carbapenemase type; follow IDSA AMR guidance.
• STEC (EHEC): supportive care; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents because of the risk of HUS.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text: Food and water hygiene, hand hygiene, minimising and promptly removing urinary catheters, and antimicrobial stewardship.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain; pyelonephritis adds fever and flank pain.
• ETEC: watery traveller's diarrhoea without fever; EHEC: bloody diarrhoea with little or no fever.
• HUS (haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury) follows EHEC, mostly in children.
• Neonatal meningitis and sepsis in the first weeks of life.
• Biliary and intra-abdominal sepsis from gut translocation.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• ESBLs (mainly CTX-M) and plasmid AmpC.
• Carbapenemases: KPC, NDM, OXA-48.
• Widespread fluoroquinolone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance.
• Resistance genes spread on plasmids between Enterobacterales.

pearls: Pink on MacConkey (lactose fermenter) and indole-positive: E. coli.
Avoid antibiotics in EHEC O157:H7 diarrhoea; HUS can follow haemorrhagic colitis, especially in children.
Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, except in pregnancy and before urological procedures with mucosal trauma.
references: Kaper JB, Nataro JP, Mobley HLT. Pathogenic Escherichia coli. Nat Rev Microbiol 2004;2:123-140.
Gupta K et al. IDSA/ESCMID guideline for acute uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women. Clin Infect Dis 2011;52:e103-e120.
Tamma PD et al. IDSA guidance on the treatment of antimicrobial-resistant Gram-negative infections. Clin Infect Dis 2024.

organisms.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
organisms.tagline: Opportunistic, intrinsically resistant pathogen of ventilated, neutropenic, burn and cystic fibrosis patients.
diseases: Chronic lung infection in cystic fibrosis
Otitis externa and malignant otitis externa

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative, aerobic, non-lactose-fermenting bacillus; oxidase-positive and motile (polar flagellum).
• Pyocyanin (blue-green) and pyoverdine (yellow-green) pigments; grape-like odour.
• Grows at 42 C, which helps to distinguish it from other pseudomonads.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Exotoxin A inhibits elongation factor 2 (the same target as diphtheria toxin).
• Type III secretion system injects ExoS, ExoT, ExoU and ExoY.
• Alginate biofilm (mucoid phenotype in cystic fibrosis) and quorum sensing.
• Elastase, phospholipase C and pyocyanin cause tissue damage.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text: Found in moist environments such as sinks, water systems and respiratory equipment. Risk factors: neutropenia, mechanical ventilation, burns, cystic fibrosis, indwelling devices and prolonged hospitalisation. Intrinsic resistance (low outer-membrane permeability, efflux pumps, chromosomal AmpC) is compounded by acquired resistance, including loss of OprD and carbapenemases.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Culture of the relevant site, with susceptibility testing on every isolate.
• Difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR) means non-susceptibility to piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, aztreonam, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin, ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• An anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam is the backbone: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, ceftazidime or meropenem, chosen by susceptibility.
• Combination therapy is not routinely needed once susceptibility is known.
• Ciprofloxacin is the main oral option.
• DTR isolates: ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam or imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam are preferred; cefiderocol is an alternative.
• Inhaled tobramycin is used for chronic cystic fibrosis infection.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text: Hand hygiene, device-care bundles, control of water and environmental sources, and contact precautions for resistant strains.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia.
• Neutropenic bacteraemia with ecthyma gangrenosum: painless black necrotic eschar with surrounding erythema.
• Burn wound infection: blue-green discharge with a sweet, grape-like odour.
• Cystic fibrosis: chronic lung infection with mucoid, alginate-producing strains.
• Otitis externa (swimmer's ear) and malignant otitis externa in older diabetic patients, with skull base osteomyelitis and cranial nerve palsy.
• Hot-tub folliculitis; catheter-associated urinary infection; keratitis in contact-lens wearers.
• Osteomyelitis after foot puncture wounds through footwear; endocarditis in injection drug users.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsically resistant to ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, first- and second-generation cephalosporins, ceftriaxone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and tetracyclines (low outer-membrane permeability, efflux pumps, chromosomal AmpC).
• Acquired: efflux up-regulation (MexAB-OprM), loss of the OprD porin (carbapenem resistance), AmpC derepression during therapy, ESBLs, carbapenemases (VIM, IMP, NDM, KPC).
• Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes and gyrA mutations cause aminoglycoside and fluoroquinolone resistance.
• Resistance can emerge during treatment, so repeat cultures if the patient is not improving.
• Difficult-to-treat resistance: newer agents such as ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, imipenem-relebactam or cefiderocol, guided by susceptibility testing.
• Biofilms in cystic fibrosis and device infections make eradication hard.

pearls: Oxidase-positive, non-lactose fermenter with blue-green pigment and a grape-like odour.
Think Pseudomonas in neutropenic fever, ventilator-associated pneumonia, burns, hot-tub folliculitis and ecthyma gangrenosum.
Ceftriaxone and ertapenem have no reliable anti-pseudomonal activity.
references: Tamma PD et al. IDSA guidance on the treatment of antimicrobial-resistant Gram-negative infections. Clin Infect Dis 2024.

Qin S et al. Pseudomonas aeruginosa: pathogenesis, virulence factors, antibiotic resistance, interaction with host, technology advances and emerging therapeutics. Signal Transduct Target Ther 2022;7:199.

organisms.name: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
organisms.tagline: Slow-growing intracellular pathogen causing granulomatous disease; a leading infectious cause of death worldwide.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Obligate aerobe, non-motile, non-spore-forming bacillus with a lipid-rich cell wall containing mycolic acids.
• Acid-fast on Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun stain; auramine-rhodamine fluorescence is used for screening.
• Very slow growth (doubling about 15-20 h): Lowenstein-Jensen solid medium takes 3-8 weeks; liquid culture (MGIT) is faster.
• Niacin-positive and nitrate reductase-positive.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) and mycolic acids protect against killing and promote granuloma formation.
• Sulfatides inhibit phagosome-lysosome fusion.
• ESX-1 secretion system (ESAT-6, CFP-10) supports intracellular survival and tissue damage.
• The cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity response drives caseous necrosis.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text: Spread by airborne droplet nuclei. An estimated quarter of the world's population has been infected. Progression to disease is most likely with HIV, immunosuppression (anti-TNF therapy, corticosteroids), diabetes, malnutrition, silicosis, chronic kidney disease and young age.

sections.title: Clinical Syndromes
sections.text:
• Primary TB: Ghon complex, often asymptomatic.
• Reactivation TB: apical cavitary disease with cough, haemoptysis, night sweats, fever and weight loss.
• Extrapulmonary: lymph nodes, pleura, bone and spine, meninges, genitourinary tract, pericardium.
• Miliary TB: haematogenous spread with a millet-seed pattern on chest X-ray.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Sputum acid-fast smear and culture, with a rapid molecular test (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra) that also detects rifampicin resistance.
• Chest radiograph: apical infiltrates and cavitation.
• Latent infection: IGRA or tuberculin skin test; neither separates latent from active disease.
• Always obtain drug-susceptibility testing.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB: 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol (HRZE), then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin.
• Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) with isoniazid and monitor liver function.
• TB meningitis and bone TB need longer courses; follow current national guidance. Corticosteroids are indicated in TB meningitis and TB pericarditis.
• A 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen is an option for eligible patients with drug-susceptible disease.
• MDR/RR-TB: all-oral regimens such as BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin) for 6 months per WHO guidance.
• Latent TB: short rifamycin-based regimens (3HP, 4R or 3HR) per local guidance.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text: BCG vaccine (protects mainly against severe childhood TB), airborne isolation of infectious patients, contact tracing and treatment of latent infection in high-risk groups.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• MDR-TB is resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin; rifampin-resistant TB is treated like MDR-TB; XDR-TB adds fluoroquinolone and bedaquiline or linezolid resistance.
• Main mutations: rpoB (rifampin), katG and inhA (isoniazid), embB (ethambutol), pncA (pyrazinamide), gyrA (fluoroquinolones).
• Causes: incomplete or non-adherent treatment, inadequate regimens, and direct transmission of resistant strains.
• Detection: Xpert MTB/RIF identifies rpoB mutations; line probe assays, whole genome sequencing and phenotypic susceptibility testing confirm the pattern.
• Treatment: WHO now recommends shorter all-oral regimens, such as BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin), under specialist supervision.
• Never add a single drug to a failing regimen; use directly observed therapy to protect adherence.

pearls: Rifampicin: orange body fluids and many drug interactions. Isoniazid: neuropathy and hepatitis. Pyrazinamide: hyperuricaemia. Ethambutol: optic neuritis.
A negative smear does not exclude TB; use culture or molecular testing.
Test every person with TB for HIV.
references: Nahid P et al. Official ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA clinical practice guidelines: treatment of drug-susceptible tuberculosis. Clin Infect Dis 2016;63:e147-e195.
Pai M et al. Tuberculosis. Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16076.
WHO. Consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis: treatment. Geneva: World Health Organization.

organisms.name: Streptococcus pyogenes
organisms.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in chains (Group A Streptococcus)
organisms.tagline: Beta-haemolytic Group A Streptococcus causing pharyngitis, skin infection and invasive disease, with post-infectious rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive cocci in chains; catalase-negative.
• Beta-haemolytic on blood agar (complete clearing), Lancefield group A.
• Bacitracin-sensitive and PYR-positive, which separates it from other beta-haemolytic streptococci.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• M protein: antiphagocytic, the basis of serotyping, and linked to rheumatic fever through molecular mimicry.
• Hyaluronic acid capsule resembles host tissue and is poorly immunogenic.
• Streptolysin O (oxygen-labile, drives the ASO response) and streptolysin S.
• Pyrogenic exotoxins SpeA, SpeB and SpeC act as superantigens (scarlet fever, toxic shock).
• Streptokinase, DNases and hyaluronidase promote spread through tissue.
• C5a peptidase inactivates complement chemotaxis.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Humans are the only reservoir; spread by respiratory droplets and direct contact with skin lesions.
• Pharyngitis peaks in school-age children (5 to 15 years) in winter and spring; impetigo is more common in warm, humid and low-resource settings.
• Rheumatic heart disease remains a major cause of cardiac disease in low- and middle-income countries.
• Invasive disease is more frequent in older adults, diabetes, injection drug use, the postpartum period and after varicella.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Pharyngitis: sudden sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, no cough.
• Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor.
• Erysipelas: raised, sharply demarcated red plaque; cellulitis is deeper and less defined.
• Necrotizing fasciitis: pain out of proportion to the skin findings, rapid spread, shock.
• Rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis only, not skin infection; glomerulonephritis can follow throat or skin infection.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Rapid antigen detection test; a negative test in children should be backed up by throat culture.
• Throat culture on blood agar remains the reference method.
• Anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B document recent infection; anti-DNase B is better after skin infection.
• Necrotizing fasciitis is a clinical and surgical diagnosis: do not wait for imaging.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Penicillin V or amoxicillin remains the drug of choice; penicillin resistance has never been documented.
• Non-severe penicillin allergy: cephalexin. Severe allergy: clindamycin or a macrolide (resistance varies locally).
• Necrotizing fasciitis and toxic shock: urgent surgical debridement, penicillin plus clindamycin to suppress toxin production, and consider IVIG.
• Treatment of pharyngitis within 9 days of onset prevents rheumatic fever but does not prevent glomerulonephritis.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Macrolide and clindamycin resistance are rising in many regions.
• Tetracycline resistance is common, so doxycycline is not reliable.
• Penicillin and beta-lactam susceptibility remains universal.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Secondary prophylaxis with long-acting benzathine penicillin after rheumatic fever.
• Close contact prophylaxis is considered in selected invasive cases.
• No licensed vaccine.

pearls: Rheumatic fever follows throat infection; glomerulonephritis can follow throat or skin.
Pain out of proportion on a red limb is necrotizing fasciitis until proven otherwise.
Clindamycin is added in severe disease because it works on toxin synthesis, not only on killing.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Shulman ST et al. IDSA guideline for group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Clin Infect Dis 2012
Stevens DL et al. IDSA guideline for skin and soft tissue infections. Clin Infect Dis 2014

organisms.name: Klebsiella pneumoniae
organisms.tagline: Encapsulated Enterobacterales causing healthcare-associated pneumonia, urinary and bloodstream infection, and hypervirulent liver abscess; carbapenem resistance is a global threat.
diseases: Pneumonia in alcohol use disorder and diabetes

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated bacilli; lactose fermenter with mucoid colonies.
• Oxidase-negative, urease-positive, indole-negative (distinguishes it from E. coli).

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Thick polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis and complement.
• Hypermucoviscous phenotype in hypervirulent strains (positive string test).
• Siderophores (enterobactin, and yersiniabactin or aerobactin in hypervirulent strains).
• Type 1 and type 3 fimbriae support adhesion and biofilm formation.
• Lipopolysaccharide endotoxin.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Colonizes the gut and, in hospital, the hands and equipment around ventilated and catheterized patients.
• A leading cause of healthcare-associated pneumonia, urinary and bloodstream infection, especially in intensive care and neonatal units.
• Hypervirulent lineages emerged in East Asia and are now reported worldwide.
• Carbapenem-resistant strains are endemic in parts of Southern Europe, South Asia, Latin America and the United States, with KPC and NDM varying by region.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Classic community pneumonia: upper-lobe consolidation with 'currant jelly' sputum and cavitation, mostly in alcohol use disorder and diabetes.
• Hospital: ventilator-associated pneumonia, catheter UTI, line infection.
• Hypervirulent strains: community liver abscess, with metastatic endophthalmitis or meningitis, seen especially in East Asia and in people with diabetes.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Culture of sputum, urine, blood or aspirates with susceptibility testing.
• Phenotypic ESBL and carbapenemase detection, and molecular tests for KPC, NDM and OXA-48.
• Imaging for liver abscess; always assess for metastatic foci.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Intrinsic resistance to ampicillin (chromosomal SHV beta-lactamase).
• ESBL producers: carbapenem.
• KPC producers: ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam or imipenem-relebactam.
• Metallo-beta-lactamase (NDM) producers: ceftazidime-avibactam with aztreonam, or cefiderocol.
• Polymyxins and tigecycline are last-line options with major limits.
• Liver abscess needs drainage as well as antibiotics.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsic: ampicillin and amoxicillin.
• Acquired: ESBLs, AmpC, carbapenemases (KPC, NDM, OXA-48), and colistin resistance.
• Hypervirulent strains were historically susceptible but convergence with resistance is now reported.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Contact precautions and screening of high-risk patients.
• Antibiotic stewardship, especially carbapenem sparing.
• Bundles for ventilator and catheter care.

pearls: Mucoid lactose-fermenting colonies with a positive string test point to hypervirulent K. pneumoniae.
Klebsiella liver abscess: always look for eye and central nervous system spread.
Carbapenem choice depends on the carbapenemase type, so identify it.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
IDSA guidance on treatment of antimicrobial-resistant gram-negative infections (current version)
Local antimicrobial guidelines and susceptibility data

organisms.name: Neisseria meningitidis
organisms.tagline: Encapsulated diplococcus causing meningitis and rapidly fatal meningococcaemia, with outbreaks in adolescents, close-living groups and the Hajj.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative diplococci, oxidase-positive and catalase-positive.
• Grows on chocolate or Thayer-Martin agar in CO2.
• Ferments glucose and maltose (N. gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only).
• Carried in the nasopharynx of about 10% of healthy people.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Polysaccharide capsule (serogroups A, B, C, W, Y, X) resists phagocytosis.
• Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) endotoxin drives shock, DIC and purpura.
• Pili mediate attachment; IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA.
• Factor H binding protein evades complement.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Humans are the only reservoir; carried in the nasopharynx by about 10% of people, with the highest carriage in adolescents and young adults.
• Spread by respiratory droplets and close, prolonged contact (households, dormitories, military barracks).
• Disease peaks in infants and in adolescents aged about 16 to 23, in late winter and early spring.
• The African meningitis belt has epidemic disease in the dry season; serogroup distribution varies (B and C in Europe and the Americas, W and X in parts of Africa, W associated with the Hajj).

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Meningitis: fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered mental state.
• Meningococcaemia: abrupt fever, petechial to purpuric rash, hypotension and shock; may occur without meningitis.
• Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: bilateral adrenal haemorrhage with refractory shock.
• Higher risk with terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9), asplenia, and crowded living.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Lumbar puncture if no contraindication: CSF Gram stain, culture, cell count, glucose and protein.
• Blood cultures before antibiotics, but never delay treatment for them.
• PCR on CSF or blood; scrape of purpuric lesions may show diplococci.
• Test for complement deficiency after recurrent or unusual-serogroup disease.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Empirical therapy is a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), started immediately.
• Penicillin G is an option once susceptibility is confirmed.
• Adjunctive dexamethasone is given with suspected bacterial meningitis per guidelines.
• Intensive care for shock, with fluids and vasopressors.
• Droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective therapy.

sections.title: Prophylaxis and Vaccines
sections.text:
• Close contacts receive a single dose of ciprofloxacin, or rifampin, or ceftriaxone (choice depends on age and pregnancy).
• Quadrivalent conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) for adolescents, asplenia, complement deficiency, and pilgrims to the Hajj.
• Serogroup B vaccines (4CMenB, MenB-FHbp) for at-risk groups and outbreaks.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Reduced penicillin susceptibility occurs in some regions.
• Ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates have been reported, so check local patterns.
• Ceftriaxone resistance is very rare.

pearls: Petechial rash with fever is a meningococcal emergency: give antibiotics before imaging or lumbar puncture if delayed.
Recurrent meningococcal disease suggests terminal complement deficiency.
Close contacts need prophylaxis the same day.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Tunkel AR et al. IDSA guidelines for bacterial meningitis. Clin Infect Dis 2004
Local public health guidance on contact prophylaxis

organisms.name: Haemophilus influenzae
organisms.tagline: Fastidious coccobacillus: encapsulated type b caused childhood meningitis and epiglottitis before vaccination, while non-typeable strains drive otitis media and COPD exacerbations.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Small Gram-negative coccobacilli, facultative anaerobe.
• Needs factor X (haemin) and factor V (NAD): grows on chocolate agar, not on plain blood agar.
• Shows satellite growth around S. aureus on blood agar.
• Six capsular types (a to f); type b has the PRP capsule, and non-typeable strains are unencapsulated.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Type b capsule (polyribosyl ribitol phosphate) prevents phagocytosis.
• IgA protease cleaves secretory IgA.
• Pili and adhesins for mucosal colonization; lipooligosaccharide endotoxin.
• Biofilm formation drives chronic and recurrent infection.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Humans are the only reservoir; non-typeable strains colonize the nasopharynx of most healthy people.
• Type b disease has fallen dramatically where the conjugate vaccine is routine, but it persists where vaccine coverage is low.
• Invasive non-typeable disease is now the dominant form in vaccinated populations, mostly in older adults, neonates and people with chronic lung disease.
• Spread by respiratory droplets and direct contact.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Hib meningitis: fever, neck stiffness, irritability in unvaccinated children; sensorineural hearing loss is a classic complication.
• Epiglottitis: drooling, muffled voice, tripod posture and stridor; the airway can close suddenly.
• Non-typeable: otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, and pneumonia in COPD.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Gram stain and culture on chocolate agar; X and V factor requirement confirms identity.
• Blood and CSF cultures in invasive disease; PCR and capsular typing where available.
• Epiglottitis: secure the airway first; lateral neck X-ray may show the thumb sign, but never delay airway management.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Invasive disease: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime.
• Otitis media or sinusitis: high-dose amoxicillin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate if beta-lactamase producers are likely.
• Alternatives: doxycycline, or respiratory fluoroquinolones in adults.
• Epiglottitis: airway protection by an experienced clinician plus ceftriaxone.
• Dexamethasone adjunct is considered in childhood Hib meningitis.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Beta-lactamase production (TEM-1) in a substantial proportion of isolates.
• BLNAR strains have altered PBP3 and resist ampicillin without a beta-lactamase.
• Check local susceptibility.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Hib conjugate vaccine in the routine childhood schedule, which has nearly eliminated type b disease.
• Rifampin prophylaxis for household contacts when an unvaccinated child under 4 is present.
• No vaccine yet for non-typeable strains.

pearls: Chocolate agar plus X and V factors and satellitism identify H. influenzae.
Epiglottitis is now rare but remains an airway emergency.
Hib vaccine cut invasive disease in children by over 90%.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Local childhood immunisation and antimicrobial guidelines
Tunkel AR et al. IDSA guidelines for bacterial meningitis. Clin Infect Dis 2004

organisms.name: Salmonella enterica
organisms.tagline: Typhoidal serovars cause enteric fever; non-typhoidal serovars cause food-borne gastroenteritis and invasive disease in vulnerable hosts.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative bacilli; motile; non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey.
• Produces H2S: black colonies on Salmonella-Shigella and XLD agar.
• Typhoidal serovars (Typhi, Paratyphi A, B, C) infect only humans; non-typhoidal serovars (Enteritidis, Typhimurium) have animal reservoirs.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Vi capsular antigen of S. Typhi resists phagocytosis and complement.
• Type III secretion systems (SPI-1 and SPI-2) invade M cells and survive in macrophages.
• Endotoxin and flagellar antigens (O, H and Vi).

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Typhoid and paratyphoid are spread by the faecal-oral route through contaminated food and water; humans are the only reservoir.
• Typhoid burden is highest in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, with roughly 9 million cases and over 100,000 deaths a year.
• Non-typhoidal serovars come from poultry, eggs, meat, fresh produce and reptiles, causing food-borne outbreaks worldwide.
• In sub-Saharan Africa, invasive non-typhoidal disease affects children with malaria or malnutrition and adults with HIV.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Typhoid: stepwise rising fever, headache, relative bradycardia, constipation then diarrhoea, rose spots, hepatosplenomegaly.
• Complications in week 3: intestinal bleeding and perforation.
• Non-typhoidal: diarrhoea, fever and cramps for 3 to 7 days; spreads to blood in infants, elderly, HIV and sickle cell disease.
• Sickle cell disease predisposes to Salmonella osteomyelitis.
• Some patients become chronic gallbladder carriers.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Blood culture is positive in the first week; bone marrow culture is the most sensitive.
• Stool culture becomes positive later; urine and duodenal samples are options.
• Widal test is unreliable and should not be used alone.
• Test for HIV and haemoglobinopathies in recurrent or invasive non-typhoidal disease.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Typhoid: azithromycin, ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone, chosen by the region of acquisition.
• Fluoroquinolone resistance is very common for South Asian isolates; extensively drug-resistant typhoid (Pakistan) needs azithromycin or a carbapenem.
• Non-typhoidal gastroenteritis in healthy people: oral rehydration, no antibiotics.
• Antibiotics for non-typhoidal infection in infants, older adults, immunocompromised patients, sickle cell disease or invasive disease.
• Chronic carriers: prolonged antibiotic therapy and sometimes cholecystectomy.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Multidrug-resistant typhoid (ampicillin, chloramphenicol, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).
• Fluoroquinolone resistance (gyrA mutations) and extended-spectrum cephalosporin resistance are increasing.
• Check regional patterns before choosing empirical therapy.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Safe water, sanitation and food hygiene; thorough cooking of poultry and eggs.
• Typhoid vaccines: Vi polysaccharide, oral Ty21a, and typhoid conjugate vaccine.
• Avoid contact with reptiles and poultry in high-risk groups; exclude carriers from food handling.

pearls: Rose spots, relative bradycardia and leucopenia suggest typhoid.
Do not treat uncomplicated non-typhoidal gastroenteritis with antibiotics in healthy adults.
Sickle cell disease leads to Salmonella osteomyelitis.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
WHO guidance on typhoid vaccines and treatment
Local antimicrobial guidelines and regional susceptibility data

organisms.name: Clostridioides difficile
organisms.tagline: Toxin-producing anaerobe and the leading cause of healthcare-associated antibiotic-related diarrhoea, ranging from mild colitis to fulminant pseudomembranous colitis.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive, strictly anaerobic, spore-forming bacilli.
• Spores survive alcohol, heat and many disinfectants, and persist on hospital surfaces for months.
• Grows on selective cycloserine-cefoxitin-fructose agar with a characteristic horse-manure odour.
• Colonizes the gut of some healthy adults and many infants without disease.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Toxin A (TcdA, enterotoxin) and toxin B (TcdB, cytotoxin) glucosylate Rho GTPases, causing cell rounding, inflammation and death.
• Binary toxin (CDT) in some strains adds virulence.
• Hypervirulent NAP1/BI/027 strain: tcdC deletion causes toxin overproduction, and it is fluoroquinolone-resistant.
• Spore formation drives transmission and relapse.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• The most common cause of healthcare-associated infectious diarrhoea in high-income countries.
• Community-onset cases account for a growing share, often after outpatient antibiotics.
• Risk rises with age over 65, long hospital stays, antibiotic exposure, and acid suppression.
• Transmission is by the faecal-oral route via spores on hands, surfaces and equipment; hypervirulent ribotype 027 caused large epidemics in North America and Europe in the 2000s.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Watery diarrhoea, lower abdominal pain, fever and leucocytosis.
• Pseudomembranous colitis: yellow-white plaques seen at colonoscopy.
• Fulminant disease: ileus, toxic megacolon, hypotension, very high white cell count, rising creatinine; diarrhoea may stop when the colon dilates.
• Risk factors: recent antibiotics (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, carbapenems), hospitalization, age over 65, proton pump inhibitors, inflammatory bowel disease and immunosuppression.
• About 20% relapse after a first episode.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Test only unformed stool (3 or more loose stools in 24 hours) from patients with symptoms.
• Two-step algorithm: glutamate dehydrogenase plus toxin immunoassay, with nucleic acid amplification (PCR) to settle disagreements.
• PCR alone detects colonization and can overcall disease.
• Do not test for cure and do not repeat tests within 7 days.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Stop the inciting antibiotic as soon as possible and review proton pump inhibitor use.
• First episode: fidaxomicin is preferred; oral vancomycin is an acceptable alternative.
• Metronidazole is only for non-severe disease when the first-line drugs are unavailable.
• Fulminant disease: oral (high dose) vancomycin plus intravenous metronidazole, rectal vancomycin if ileus is present, and early surgical review for colectomy.
• Recurrence: fidaxomicin or a tapered-pulsed vancomycin regimen; faecal microbiota transplantation or approved microbiota-based products for multiple recurrences.
• Avoid antimotility drugs in active colitis.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Fluoroquinolone resistance in epidemic ribotype 027 favours its spread.
• Reduced metronidazole susceptibility has been reported in some regions.
• Vancomycin and fidaxomicin resistance is rare.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Antibiotic stewardship is the most effective measure.
• Contact precautions with a private room and gloves and gowns.
• Wash hands with soap and water, because alcohol gel does not kill spores.
• Sporicidal environmental cleaning, such as chlorine-based agents.
• Isolate until at least 48 hours after diarrhoea stops, per local policy.

pearls: Alcohol hand gel does not kill C. difficile spores: use soap and water.
Do not test formed stool or test for cure.
Fidaxomicin lowers recurrence compared with vancomycin.
references: McDonald LC et al. IDSA/SHEA clinical practice guidelines for C. difficile infection (2017 update and 2021 focused update). Clin Infect Dis
Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Local infection prevention policy

organisms.name: Legionella pneumophila
organisms.tagline: Waterborne intracellular pathogen causing Legionnaires' disease, a severe atypical pneumonia with extrapulmonary features, and mild Pontiac fever.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Thin Gram-negative bacilli that stain poorly with Gram stain; visualized by silver stain (Dieterle) or direct fluorescent antibody.
• Aerobic, facultative intracellular organism of freshwater, growing inside amoebae and biofilms.
• Needs buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar with iron and L-cysteine; does not grow on routine media.
• Serogroup 1 of L. pneumophila causes most disease.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Dot/Icm type IV secretion system delivers effectors that create a replicative vacuole inside macrophages.
• Survives and multiplies in alveolar macrophages and in free-living amoebae.
• Flagella and pili aid colonization of lung tissue; biofilm formation protects the organism in water systems.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Found in natural freshwater and in man-made water systems such as cooling towers, hot water systems and spa pools.
• Cases are sporadic or cluster in outbreaks, with more cases in summer and early autumn.
• Incidence has been rising in North America and Europe; case fatality is about 5 to 10% overall, higher in hospital-acquired disease.
• Travel-associated and healthcare-associated clusters are common.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Transmission by inhaling aerosolized water (cooling towers, showers, hot tubs, humidifiers, decorative fountains); no person-to-person spread.
• Pneumonia with high fever, dry cough, dyspnoea, headache and confusion.
• Extrapulmonary clues: diarrhoea, relative bradycardia, hyponatraemia, raised liver enzymes and creatine kinase, haematuria.
• Risk factors: age over 50, smoking, chronic lung disease, immunosuppression, recent travel or hotel stay, and healthcare exposure.
• Pontiac fever: self-limited fever and myalgia without pneumonia after a high-dose exposure.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Urinary antigen test is fast but detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1.
• Lower respiratory culture on BCYE agar or PCR (best sensitivity and covers other species and serogroups) in suspected cases.
• Gram stain shows many neutrophils but few or no bacteria.
• Chest imaging shows patchy to lobar consolidation that can progress despite beta-lactam treatment.
• Report confirmed cases to public health for source investigation.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) or azithromycin, which penetrate cells.
• Beta-lactams, including cephalosporins, and aminoglycosides do not work against intracellular organisms.
• Severe or immunocompromised cases: consider fluoroquinolone with or without a macrolide, per local guidance.
• Treatment duration is typically 7 to 10 days, longer in severe or immunosuppressed cases.
• Hospital water systems need remediation when a case is acquired there.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsically unresponsive to beta-lactams in practice because the organism lives inside cells.
• Acquired resistance to macrolides and fluoroquinolones is rare, but treatment failure should prompt culture and susceptibility review.
• Empirical cover for atypicals in community pneumonia protocols includes Legionella.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Water system management plans: temperature control, disinfection and flushing of low-use outlets.
• Regular maintenance of cooling towers, hot tubs and decorative fountains.
• No vaccine.

pearls: Pneumonia plus diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and relative bradycardia should prompt Legionella testing.
Urinary antigen misses non-serogroup 1 and non-pneumophila species, so send PCR or culture too.
Beta-lactams fail: use a fluoroquinolone or azithromycin.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Metlay JP et al. ATS/IDSA guideline for community-acquired pneumonia. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019
Local public health guidance on Legionella control

organisms.name: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
organisms.morphology: Pleomorphic bacteria lacking a cell wall
organisms.tagline: Smallest free-living bacterium, causing 'walking pneumonia' and tracheobronchitis in older children and young adults, with notable extrapulmonary complications.
diseases: Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis, Stevens-Johnson-like syndrome

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• No cell wall: not visible on Gram stain and intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams.
• Membrane contains cholesterol (taken from the host); grows slowly on specialised media such as SP4, which makes culture impractical.
• Attaches to respiratory epithelium and remains extracellular.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• P1 adhesin binds sialylated receptors on respiratory epithelium and damages cilia.
• Community-acquired respiratory distress syndrome (CARDS) toxin.
• Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide production injure host cells; immune-mediated injury drives much of the illness.
• Molecular mimicry with the I antigen on red cells produces cold agglutinins.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Accounts for roughly 15 to 20% of community-acquired pneumonia, with epidemics every 3 to 7 years.
• Most common in school-age children and young adults; spread by respiratory droplets with an incubation of 1 to 3 weeks.
• Outbreaks occur in schools, households, military camps and other crowded settings.
• Cases fell during COVID-19 restrictions and rebounded afterwards.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Gradual onset of low-grade fever, headache, malaise, sore throat and persistent dry cough over 1 to 3 weeks.
• Chest X-ray often looks worse than the patient (patchy or reticulonodular infiltrates).
• Extrapulmonary: haemolytic anaemia with cold agglutinins (IgM), erythema multiforme and mucositis, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome and arthralgia.
• Peaks in school-age children and young adults, with outbreaks in crowded settings and epidemic cycles every few years.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• PCR of throat or nasopharyngeal swab is the preferred test.
• Serology (IgM, or a rise in IgG paired samples) is helpful but slow.
• Cold agglutinin titre is non-specific and supports the diagnosis only.
• Gram stain and routine culture are unhelpful.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Macrolides (azithromycin) are first-line for children and adults; doxycycline is an alternative, and a respiratory fluoroquinolone is an option in adults.
• Macrolide-resistant strains (23S rRNA mutations, common in parts of Asia) are treated with doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone, with specialist advice in children.
• Beta-lactams and other cell-wall agents are ineffective.
• Mild disease often resolves without treatment; treatment shortens symptoms.
• Corticosteroids or immunomodulators are considered in severe immune-mediated complications, with specialist input.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsic resistance to all cell-wall active agents (beta-lactams, glycopeptides) and to sulfonamides.
• Acquired macrolide resistance by point mutations in the 23S rRNA gene (such as A2063G), with prevalence varying greatly by country.
• Fluoroquinolone and tetracycline resistance is rare but reported.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Droplet precautions and hand and respiratory hygiene.
• Outbreak control in schools, military settings and dormitories.
• No licensed vaccine.

pearls: Atypical pneumonia not responding to a beta-lactam: think Mycoplasma, Legionella or Chlamydia.
Cold agglutinins and haemolysis point to Mycoplasma.
Chest X-ray looks worse than the patient.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Metlay JP et al. ATS/IDSA guideline for community-acquired pneumonia. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019
Local antimicrobial guidelines and resistance data

organisms.name: Enterococcus faecalis and faecium
organisms.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains
organisms.tagline: Hardy gut commensals that cause urinary, biliary, wound and bloodstream infection and endocarditis; intrinsic resistance and vancomycin resistance (VRE) make them a leading healthcare-associated problem.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains; catalase-negative.
• Facultative anaerobe that is PYR-positive, hydrolyses esculin in the presence of 40% bile, and grows in 6.5% NaCl.
• Usually non- or alpha-haemolytic; E. faecalis causes most infections, but E. faecium is more often multidrug-resistant.
• Lancefield group D antigen.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Aggregation substance and adhesins promote colonization and biofilm formation on catheters and valves.
• Cytolysin (E. faecalis) is a haemolysin and bacteriocin.
• Gelatinase and enterococcal surface protein (Esp) aid tissue invasion and biofilm.
• Survives harsh conditions: high salt, bile, heat and many disinfectants.
• Efficient gene transfer by conjugative plasmids and transposons spreads resistance.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Normal inhabitants of the gut, and sometimes the female genital tract and oral cavity.
• Among the leading causes of healthcare-associated infection, especially in intensive care, haematology and transplant units.
• Risk factors: prolonged hospital stay, previous cephalosporin or vancomycin use, urinary catheters, abdominal surgery and immunosuppression.
• Spread on hands, equipment and surfaces; VRE prevalence varies widely by country and by hospital, and is highest for E. faecium.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Catheter-associated UTI and pyelonephritis are the commonest syndromes.
• Bacteraemia from a urinary, biliary or intra-abdominal source or from an infected line.
• Subacute endocarditis, especially in older men with a genitourinary source or in those with prosthetic valves.
• Polymicrobial intra-abdominal infection and surgical wound infection.
• Neonatal sepsis in preterm infants.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Gram stain and culture of urine, blood or tissue; identify to species level (E. faecalis versus E. faecium) and test susceptibility.
• Bile-esculin, PYR and growth in 6.5% NaCl identify the genus.
• Molecular van gene tests or phenotypic MICs classify VRE.
• In enterococcal bacteraemia, search for endocarditis and drain any source, and repeat blood cultures.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Ampicillin-susceptible isolates (mainly E. faecalis): amoxicillin or ampicillin for urinary infection and bacteraemia.
• Endocarditis: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (double beta-lactam) is preferred for E. faecalis, with ampicillin plus gentamicin as an alternative where gentamicin is safe.
• Ampicillin-resistant, vancomycin-susceptible strains: vancomycin.
• VRE: linezolid or daptomycin at higher doses (check susceptibility and site); nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin for uncomplicated VRE cystitis.
• Remove infected catheters and drain collections.
• Cephalosporins, clindamycin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are not reliable: enterococci are intrinsically resistant or appear active in vitro but fail in vivo.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsic: all cephalosporins, clindamycin, low-level aminoglycoside resistance and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (in vivo).
• Ampicillin resistance in E. faecium arises from altered PBP5 overproduction or mutation.
• vanA: high-level resistance to vancomycin and teicoplanin; vanB: vancomycin resistance with teicoplanin susceptibility; vanC is intrinsic and low-level in E. gallinarum and E. casseliflavus.
• Van genes change the cell wall precursor from D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac.
• Linezolid resistance (23S rRNA mutations, cfr, optrA) and daptomycin resistance are emerging.
• High-level gentamicin resistance rules out synergy with aminoglycosides.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Hand hygiene and contact precautions for VRE colonized or infected patients.
• Environmental cleaning of high-touch surfaces and dedicated equipment.
• Antibiotic stewardship, especially limiting cephalosporin and vancomycin use.
• Remove urinary catheters and central lines as soon as they are not needed.

pearls: Cephalosporins do not cover enterococci, a classic cause of breakthrough bacteraemia.
Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone works for E. faecalis endocarditis because of complementary PBP binding.
Always identify to species: E. faecalis is usually ampicillin-susceptible, E. faecium usually is not.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Baddour LM et al. AHA scientific statement on infective endocarditis in adults. Circulation 2015
IDSA guidance on treatment of antimicrobial-resistant infections (current version)

organisms.name: Acinetobacter baumannii
organisms.tagline: Desiccation-tolerant, multidrug-resistant opportunist causing ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream and wound infection in intensive care units; carbapenem resistance is now widespread.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative coccobacilli that may look like Gram-positive diplococci on smear.
• Strictly aerobic, non-motile, non-lactose fermenting (pale colonies on MacConkey).
• Oxidase-negative and catalase-positive, which separates it from Pseudomonas (oxidase-positive).
• Survives for weeks on dry hospital surfaces.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Outer membrane protein A (OmpA) mediates adhesion and cell death.
• Capsule, biofilm formation and desiccation tolerance support survival on surfaces and devices.
• Efflux pumps and low outer membrane permeability reduce antibiotic entry.
• Lipopolysaccharide and phospholipases; natural competence allows rapid acquisition of resistance genes.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Mainly a healthcare-associated pathogen in intensive care units and burn units.
• Risk factors: mechanical ventilation, prolonged stay, previous broad-spectrum antibiotics, invasive devices and burns.
• Gained notoriety in military wounded in Iraq and Afghanistan.
• Carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) is endemic in many regions of Asia, the Middle East, Southern Europe and Latin America.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Ventilator-associated pneumonia is the commonest syndrome, with high mortality.
• Bacteraemia from lines, the lungs or wounds.
• Wound and burn infection; osteomyelitis after trauma.
• Meningitis after neurosurgery or with external ventricular drains.
• Isolation from sputum may represent colonization, so interpret together with the clinical picture.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Culture of sputum, blood, wound or CSF; identify to species with MALDI-TOF.
• Susceptibility testing is essential because patterns vary between units.
• Molecular detection of OXA carbapenemase genes where available.
• Differentiate colonization from infection to avoid unnecessary treatment.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Carbapenem (meropenem or imipenem) if susceptible.
• Carbapenem-resistant disease: high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam (sulbactam has intrinsic activity) combined with at least one other active agent, such as polymyxin B, minocycline or tigecycline, or cefiderocol.
• Sulbactam-durlobactam is an option for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia.
• Polymyxins have toxicity (kidney and nerve) and limited lung penetration; tigecycline is not suitable for bloodstream infection or pneumonia as monotherapy.
• Source control and device removal are part of treatment.
• Combination therapy is often used, with specialist infectious diseases advice.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsic: ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, first- and second-generation cephalosporins, ertapenem and chloramphenicol, among others.
• OXA-23, OXA-24/40 and OXA-58 carbapenemases are most common; NDM and other metallo-beta-lactamases also occur.
• Chromosomal AmpC (ADC), efflux pumps, porin loss and altered PBPs.
• Colistin resistance via pmrAB mutations and lipid A modification.
• Resistance genes cluster on mobile genetic islands.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Strict hand hygiene and contact precautions for CRAB.
• Environmental cleaning with attention to high-touch surfaces and shared equipment.
• Cohorting of colonized and infected patients and screening in outbreaks.
• Antibiotic stewardship, particularly limiting carbapenem use, and care bundles for ventilators and catheters.

pearls: Oxidase-negative Gram-negative coccobacilli in a ventilated patient: think Acinetobacter.
Sulbactam is active on its own against Acinetobacter, which is why it is used at high doses.
Colonization is common: treat infection, not a positive culture.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
IDSA guidance on the treatment of antimicrobial-resistant gram-negative infections (current version)
Local antimicrobial guidelines and susceptibility data

organisms.name: Vibrio cholerae
organisms.morphology: Curved Gram-negative bacilli (comma-shaped) with a single polar flagellum
organisms.tagline: Toxigenic waterborne pathogen causing profuse rice-water diarrhoea and rapid dehydration; epidemics follow poor sanitation and unsafe water.
diseases: Non-O1 and non-O139 gastroenteritis and wound infection (rare)

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Curved Gram-negative bacilli, highly motile with a single polar flagellum.
• Oxidase-positive; ferments glucose and sucrose, so it makes yellow colonies on TCBS agar.
• Tolerates alkaline conditions (alkaline peptone water enrichment) and is killed by gastric acid.
• O1 (classical and El Tor biotypes) and O139 serogroups cause epidemic cholera.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Cholera toxin (encoded by the CTX phage) is an AB5 toxin: the A subunit ADP-ribosylates Gs, raising cAMP and driving chloride and water secretion.
• Toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP) mediates colonization and is the receptor for CTX phage.
• Mucinase, neuraminidase and flagellar motility help penetrate the mucus layer.
• Non-invasive: the organism stays in the lumen, so there is no blood or pus in the stool.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Transmitted through contaminated water and food (including raw shellfish); outbreaks follow floods, conflict and displacement.
• Endemic in South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and parts of the Middle East; the seventh pandemic (El Tor) began in 1961.
• Major outbreaks: Haiti (2010 onwards) and Yemen (2016 onwards).
• Estimated 1.3 to 4 million cases and 21,000 to 143,000 deaths per year worldwide.
• Most infections are mild or asymptomatic, but they can still spread the organism.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Incubation from a few hours to 5 days.
• Sudden painless watery diarrhoea, 'rice-water' stool, with vomiting; fluid loss can reach 1 litre per hour.
• Dehydration: sunken eyes, absent skin turgor, thirst, oliguria, hypotension and shock.
• Hypokalaemia (cramps, arrhythmia) and metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss.
• Without treatment, death can occur within hours; with prompt rehydration, mortality is under 1%.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Clinical diagnosis in an outbreak setting; start rehydration immediately.
• Stool or rectal swab culture on TCBS agar; dark-field microscopy shows darting motility.
• Rapid dipstick tests for O1 and O139 antigen are useful for field surveillance.
• PCR for the ctxA gene confirms toxigenic strains.
• Report suspected cases to public health authorities.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Rehydration is the lifesaving treatment: oral rehydration solution for mild and moderate dehydration, and intravenous Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration.
• Monitor fluid balance and replace ongoing losses; correct potassium and acidosis.
• Antibiotics shorten illness and reduce stool volume in moderate to severe cases: single-dose azithromycin (or doxycycline in non-pregnant adults) is commonly used; follow local resistance patterns.
• Zinc supplementation for children.
• Continue feeding, and breastfeeding in infants.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Tetracycline resistance and multidrug-resistant strains carrying the SXT integrating conjugative element (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, streptomycin, chloramphenicol) are reported in many regions.
• Reduced ciprofloxacin susceptibility is common in El Tor strains.
• Azithromycin remains active in most areas, but check local surveillance.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Safe drinking water, sanitation and handwashing.
• Oral cholera vaccines (killed, two doses, or a single-dose live vaccine for travellers) are used in endemic areas, outbreaks and for travellers at risk.
• Thorough cooking of seafood and food safety.
• Household and community measures during outbreaks, plus targeted chemoprophylaxis for close contacts where recommended.

pearls: Treat the dehydration first: rehydration saves lives, and antibiotics are an adjunct.
Rice-water stool without blood or pus is classic for cholera.
Cholera toxin acts by raising cAMP, similar in effect to ETEC's heat-labile toxin.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
WHO guidance on cholera case management and oral cholera vaccines
Local public health guidance

organisms.name: Treponema pallidum
organisms.morphology: Thin, tightly coiled spirochete (too thin for Gram stain)
organisms.tagline: Spirochete causing syphilis, the great imitator: a staged disease from painless chancre to late cardiovascular and neurological damage, also transmitted from mother to fetus.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Spirochete with a tight helical coil; too thin to see on Gram stain.
• Seen by dark-field microscopy, direct fluorescent antibody or silver stains (Warthin-Starry).
• Cannot be grown on routine culture media; very slow dividing (about 30 hours).
• Fragile outside the host: killed by drying, heat and many disinfectants.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Few surface-exposed outer membrane proteins, which helps it evade antibody (stealth pathogen).
• Antigenic variation of the TprK protein allows immune escape.
• Corkscrew motility from periplasmic endoflagella lets it cross tissues and mucosa.
• Hyaluronidase and adhesins promote spread and attachment.
• Lipoproteins trigger inflammation; endarteritis and perivascular plasma-cell infiltration cause much of the tissue damage.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Spread mainly by sexual contact through mucosal or skin lesions, and across the placenta (at any stage of pregnancy); rarely by blood transfusion.
• Humans are the only reservoir.
• Rising incidence in many countries, particularly in men who have sex with men, with growing rates among heterosexual adults and in congenital syphilis.
• HIV co-infection is common, and each infection makes the other more likely.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Primary: a single painless, indurated ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation about 3 weeks after exposure, with painless regional lymph nodes; heals by itself within weeks.
• Secondary (weeks to months later): diffuse maculopapular rash, often involving the palms and soles, mucous patches, condylomata lata, generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise and patchy alopecia.
• Latent: no symptoms but positive serology; early latent is under 1 year from infection and late latent is more than 1 year or unknown.
• Tertiary (years later): gummas, cardiovascular syphilis (aortitis, aortic aneurysm and regurgitation) and neurosyphilis.
• Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage: meningitis, stroke, tabes dorsalis (ataxia, lightning pains, Argyll Robertson pupil) and general paresis.
• Congenital: stillbirth, rash, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, bone changes; late signs include Hutchinson teeth, interstitial keratitis, eighth nerve deafness and saddle nose.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Dark-field microscopy or PCR of fluid from a moist lesion in early disease.
• Serology is the main tool: a nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL) measures disease activity and titres, and a treponemal test (TPPA, FTA-ABS, EIA) confirms; use both.
• Treponemal tests usually stay positive for life, while nontreponemal titres fall with successful treatment.
• False-positive nontreponemal tests occur in pregnancy, lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, viral infection and injection drug use; a very high titre can give a false negative (prozone effect).
• CSF VDRL and cell count when neurological, eye or ear symptoms are present.
• Test all patients for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Penicillin is the treatment of choice for every stage.
• Primary, secondary and early latent syphilis: a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G.
• Late latent, unknown duration and tertiary syphilis without nervous system involvement: three weekly doses of benzathine penicillin G.
• Neurosyphilis, ocular and otic syphilis: intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10 to 14 days.
• Pregnancy: penicillin only, with desensitization if allergic; congenital syphilis in newborns is treated with intravenous penicillin.
• Penicillin-allergic non-pregnant adults: doxycycline for 14 days (early) or 28 days (late), after specialist advice.
• Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever, headache and myalgia within 24 hours of the first dose) is self-limited; warn patients.
• Follow-up: repeat nontreponemal titres at 6 and 12 months, looking for at least a four-fold fall, and treat sexual partners.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• No penicillin resistance has ever been documented.
• Macrolide resistance (23S rRNA mutations A2058G and A2059G) is widespread, so azithromycin should not be used.
• Tetracycline resistance has not been reported.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Condoms and sexual health screening for people at risk.
• Routine antenatal screening, and rescreening in the third trimester and at delivery in high-risk groups.
• Partner notification and presumptive treatment of partners exposed within 90 days.
• Doxycycline taken after sex has been shown to reduce syphilis in selected high-risk groups, and is used under national guidance.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: A painless genital ulcer is syphilis until proven otherwise (chancroid is painful).
Rash on the palms and soles: think secondary syphilis.
Never use azithromycin for syphilis.
Pregnant women with syphilis must receive penicillin.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines (current version)
WHO guidelines on the treatment of syphilis

organisms.name: Clostridium tetani
organisms.morphology: Gram-positive spore-forming anaerobic bacilli (terminal round spores)
organisms.tagline: Soil-dwelling anaerobe whose toxin, tetanospasmin, blocks inhibitory neurotransmitters and causes painful spasms, lockjaw and autonomic instability; fully preventable by vaccination.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive, strictly anaerobic, motile bacilli.
• Round terminal spores give a drumstick or tennis-racket appearance.
• Spores live in soil, dust and animal faeces for years, and resist boiling and many disinfectants.
• Grows in dead tissue with low oxygen, such as in puncture wounds and burns.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin) is plasmid-encoded: a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP) in inhibitory interneurons.
• The toxin travels by retrograde axonal transport to the spinal cord and brainstem.
• Blocked release of GABA and glycine removes inhibition of motor neurons, causing rigidity and spasm.
• Tetanolysin is a haemolysin; the bacteria stay in the wound and do not invade tissue.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Found worldwide, with most cases in places where vaccination coverage is low.
• Neonatal tetanus follows contamination of the umbilical stump and still causes deaths in low-resource settings.
• In high-income countries cases occur in older adults, people who inject drugs and unvaccinated individuals.
• Incubation is usually 3 to 21 days; a shorter incubation and shorter time to the first spasm suggest more severe disease.
• Not spread between people; disease does not give immunity, so patients still need vaccination.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Trismus (lockjaw) is the commonest first sign, followed by risus sardonicus and neck stiffness.
• Opisthotonus, dysphagia, board-like abdominal rigidity and painful generalized spasms triggered by noise, light or touch, with preserved consciousness.
• Autonomic instability: labile blood pressure, tachycardia, sweating and arrhythmias are a major cause of death in the second week.
• Laryngospasm and respiratory failure; complications include fractures, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis and thromboembolism.
• Localized tetanus affects muscles near the wound; cephalic tetanus follows head wounds with cranial nerve palsies.
• Neonatal tetanus: poor suckling, rigidity and spasms in the first weeks of life.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Diagnosis is clinical; do not wait for laboratory confirmation.
• Wound culture is often negative and a positive culture does not prove disease.
• Spatula test: touching the posterior pharynx triggers a masseter spasm (bite) instead of a gag reflex.
• A serum antitoxin level above the protective threshold taken before immune globulin makes tetanus unlikely.
• Look for the wound, but in many patients none is found.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Admit to intensive care, in a quiet, dark room with minimal stimulation.
• Human tetanus immune globulin (given early) neutralizes circulating toxin but not toxin already bound in nerves.
• Metronidazole is the preferred antibiotic; penicillin G is an alternative, although it may worsen spasms through GABA antagonism.
• Wound cleaning and debridement.
• Spasm control: benzodiazepines, magnesium sulfate, baclofen, and neuromuscular blockade with mechanical ventilation in severe cases; secure the airway early.
• Autonomic instability: magnesium sulfate, sedation, and careful use of beta-blockers or clonidine.
• Prevent complications with nutrition and thromboprophylaxis; recovery takes weeks as nerve terminals regrow.
• Start the vaccine series during recovery.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Antibiotic resistance is not a clinical problem: metronidazole and penicillin remain active.
• Antibiotics are secondary to toxin neutralization, wound care and supportive care.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Tetanus toxoid vaccination: the primary childhood series with boosters (Td or Tdap) about every 10 years.
• Wound management: clean and debride; give a booster when the last dose was more than 10 years ago (5 years for dirty wounds).
• Dirty wound and an unknown or incomplete vaccine history: give tetanus immune globulin as well as a vaccine dose.
• Maternal immunization in pregnancy, clean delivery and cord care to prevent neonatal tetanus.

pearls: Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory neurons, so the muscles fire without opposition.
Disease does not give immunity: always vaccinate survivors.
Trismus with a clear mind and spasms triggered by touch is tetanus.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC Pink Book: Tetanus chapter
WHO position paper on tetanus vaccines

organisms.name: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
organisms.tagline: Sexually transmitted diplococcus causing urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease and disseminated infection; antibiotic resistance has narrowed treatment to few options.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative diplococci with flattened adjacent sides (kidney-bean shape), often seen inside neutrophils.
• Oxidase-positive and catalase-positive; ferments glucose only (N. meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose).
• Fastidious: grows on chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin selective medium in 5% CO2.
• No capsule, which distinguishes it from N. meningitidis.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Type IV pili mediate attachment and undergo antigenic variation, which is why no vaccine exists.
• Opa proteins promote tight adhesion and invasion; porin proteins (PorB) interfere with phagocyte killing.
• Lipooligosaccharide (LOS) endotoxin causes the intense neutrophil response and pus.
• IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA.
• Evades complement by sialylating LOS and binding factor H.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Humans are the only host; spread by sexual contact and from mother to newborn during delivery.
• WHO estimates over 80 million new infections a year in adults.
• Highest rates are in sexually active young adults and men who have sex with men.
• Co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis is common, and gonorrhoea increases HIV transmission.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Men: purulent urethral discharge and dysuria within days of exposure; complications include epididymitis.
• Women: often asymptomatic; cervicitis with discharge, then pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal scarring, infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
• Pharyngeal and rectal infection are usually asymptomatic.
• Disseminated gonococcal infection: fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and a pustular or vesicular rash, or purulent monoarthritis.
• Neonatal conjunctivitis appears 2 to 5 days after birth with severe purulent discharge and can cause corneal perforation.
• Women with complement deficiency (C5 to C9) are prone to recurrent disseminated disease.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on first-catch urine or vaginal, cervical, urethral, pharyngeal or rectal swabs is the test of choice.
• Gram stain of urethral discharge in symptomatic men shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci and is diagnostic in that setting.
• Culture on Thayer-Martin agar is still needed for susceptibility testing, particularly with treatment failure.
• In suspected disseminated disease, culture blood, joint fluid and genital sites.
• Always test for chlamydia, syphilis and HIV.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Ceftriaxone as a single intramuscular dose is the recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated infection.
• Add doxycycline when chlamydia has not been excluded.
• If ceftriaxone cannot be used: gentamicin plus azithromycin, or other options per national guidance.
• Disseminated infection and pelvic inflammatory disease need longer courses of ceftriaxone and specialist review.
• Treat all sexual partners from the last 60 days, and advise abstinence until treatment is completed.
• Retest after about 3 months, and perform a test of cure for pharyngeal infection and in treatment failure.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Resistance has developed to penicillin, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones, so none of these can be used empirically.
