• Azithromycin resistance is rising, so it is no longer recommended as monotherapy or as dual therapy partner in many guidelines.
• Ceftriaxone-resistant strains (for example the FC428 clone) have been reported in Asia, Europe and Australia, and extensively drug-resistant gonorrhoea is a global concern.
• Culture and susceptibility testing is essential for any treatment failure.
• New agents are in development.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Condoms and regular screening in those at risk.
• Partner notification and treatment.
• Eye prophylaxis for newborns where recommended.
• No vaccine yet; the serogroup B meningococcal vaccine (4CMenB) gives partial cross-protection and is used in some national programmes.

pearls: Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci on a urethral smear are diagnostic in men.
Think disseminated gonococcal infection with a sexually active young adult with migratory joint pain, tenosynovitis and pustules.
Always treat for chlamydia as well unless it has been excluded.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines (current version)
WHO guidelines on the treatment of Neisseria gonorrhoeae

organisms.name: Chlamydia trachomatis
organisms.morphology: Obligate intracellular bacterium with elementary and reticulate body forms
organisms.tagline: Obligate intracellular pathogen causing the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection, trachoma (leading infectious cause of blindness) and lymphogranuloma venereum.
diseases: Urethritis, cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Obligate intracellular bacterium that cannot grow on routine media or be seen reliably with a Gram stain.
• Life cycle: the infectious elementary body (EB) enters the cell; it turns into a metabolically active reticulate body (RB) that divides inside an inclusion; RBs turn back into EBs and are released.
• Cell wall lacks a conventional peptidoglycan layer; inclusions are seen with Giemsa or fluorescent antibody stains.
• Serovars A to C cause trachoma, D to K cause genital and neonatal infection, and L1 to L3 cause LGV.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• The elementary body attaches to and is taken up by epithelial cells.
• Inclusion membrane proteins prevent phagosome-lysosome fusion, creating a protected niche.
• Type III secretion system injects effector proteins that remodel the host cell.
• Persistent forms under immune or antibiotic pressure contribute to chronic scarring and reinfection.
• Immune-mediated damage, not direct toxicity, causes most of the long-term injury.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• The most commonly reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection in many countries, with an estimated 120 million or more new infections a year worldwide.
• Highest rates in sexually active adults under 25.
• Trachoma is spread by flies, fingers and shared cloths in communities with poor water access and crowding.
• LGV is endemic in tropical areas and has caused outbreaks of proctitis in men who have sex with men.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Often asymptomatic, especially in women.
• Urethritis with mucoid discharge and dysuria; cervicitis; pelvic inflammatory disease with tubal damage; epididymitis.
• Reactive arthritis (with urethritis and conjunctivitis) after genital infection.
• Neonatal conjunctivitis 5 to 14 days after birth; infant pneumonia at 1 to 3 months with a staccato cough and no fever.
• Trachoma: repeated follicular conjunctivitis, eyelid scarring, trichiasis (inturned lashes) and corneal opacity.
• LGV: a transient painless ulcer, then painful inguinal lymph nodes (buboes) or haemorrhagic proctocolitis.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• NAAT on first-catch urine or vaginal, cervical or urethral swabs; rectal and pharyngeal swabs when exposed.
• LGV-specific PCR identifies L serovars in rectal or bubo samples.
• Screen sexually active women under 25, and others at risk, even without symptoms.
• Culture needs cell lines and is not routine; serology has little value for genital infection.
• Test for gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Doxycycline for 7 days is first-line for uncomplicated genital and rectal infection.
• Azithromycin as a single dose is an alternative, and it is the usual choice in pregnancy.
• LGV: doxycycline for 21 days.
• Neonatal infection: oral macrolide (erythromycin or azithromycin).
• Trachoma: single-dose azithromycin, with community mass treatment as part of the SAFE strategy (surgery for trichiasis, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environmental improvement).
• Treat all partners from the last 60 days, advise abstinence until treatment is completed, and retest at about 3 months.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Clinically significant resistance is rare.
• Treatment failure occurs mostly from reinfection or non-adherence; doxycycline is more effective than azithromycin for rectal infection.
• Beta-lactam antibiotics can induce persistent forms and are not used.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Condoms, screening programmes, and partner notification and treatment.
• Eye prophylaxis for newborns where guidelines recommend it, and antenatal screening.
• Trachoma control by the SAFE strategy.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: Gonorrhoea and chlamydia often occur together, so treat for both unless one is excluded.
Urethritis, conjunctivitis and arthritis suggest reactive arthritis after chlamydia.
Infant pneumonia with a staccato cough and no fever: think chlamydia.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines (current version)
WHO guidance on trachoma elimination (SAFE strategy)

organisms.name: Listeria monocytogenes
organisms.morphology: Short Gram-positive bacilli with tumbling motility
organisms.tagline: Food-borne intracellular pathogen that grows at refrigerator temperature and causes meningitis and sepsis in neonates, pregnant women, older adults and immunocompromised patients.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Short Gram-positive, non-spore-forming bacilli; facultative anaerobe and intracellular organism.
• Tumbling motility at room temperature; umbrella-shaped growth in semi-solid agar at 25 degrees Celsius.
• Catalase-positive, narrow zone of beta-haemolysis on blood agar, and esculin hydrolysis.
• Grows at 4 degrees Celsius, so refrigeration does not stop it growing.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Internalins (InlA, InlB) bind E-cadherin and Met receptors to enter epithelial cells.
• Listeriolysin O (LLO) lyses the phagosome and releases the bacteria into the cytoplasm.
• ActA induces host actin polymerization, forming 'comet tails' that push the bacteria into neighbouring cells (cell-to-cell spread).
• Phospholipases aid escape; the PrfA regulator controls these genes.
• Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) controls infection, which explains the risk groups.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Found in soil, water, vegetation and animals; spread through contaminated food.
• Common sources: unpasteurized milk and soft cheeses, deli meats, hot dogs, smoked fish, pre-cut melon, sprouts and other ready-to-eat foods.
• Pregnant women are around ten times more likely to be infected than others.
• Rare but serious: invasive disease has a case fatality of about 20%.
• Outbreaks are often multi-state or national, and are traced by whole genome sequencing.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Healthy adults: febrile gastroenteritis within 24 hours of a large inoculum, usually self-limited.
• Invasive disease: bacteraemia and meningitis or meningoencephalitis in neonates, adults over 50, pregnancy, transplant recipients, those on steroids or TNF inhibitors, diabetes, cirrhosis and HIV.
• Brainstem infection (rhombencephalitis) with cranial nerve palsies and ataxia is characteristic; brain abscess occurs.
• Pregnancy: mild flu-like illness with risk of miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm delivery.
• Neonates: early-onset sepsis with granulomatosis infantiseptica, or late-onset meningitis.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Blood cultures and CSF culture are the mainstay; Gram stain of CSF is often negative or shows few organisms.
• Can be mistaken for diphtheroid contaminants, so always identify the isolate.
• Multiplex PCR panels detect Listeria in CSF but sensitivity is limited.
• Stool culture is not routine except in outbreaks; maternal blood cultures in pregnancy with fever.
• MRI for suspected rhombencephalitis or abscess.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Ampicillin (or penicillin G) is first-line; gentamicin is added for synergy in severe disease such as meningitis, endocarditis or bacteraemia in immunocompromised patients.
• Penicillin allergy: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
• Meropenem is an alternative for meningitis.
• Cephalosporins are not active, so empirical meningitis cover in neonates, adults over 50 and immunocompromised patients must include ampicillin.
• Duration: at least 14 to 21 days for meningitis, and longer for brain abscess or rhombencephalitis.
• Febrile gastroenteritis in healthy people usually needs no antibiotics.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins.
• Also has reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones.
• Resistance to ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is rare.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Avoid unpasteurized milk and soft cheeses, and reheat deli meats and hot dogs until steaming, particularly in pregnancy and for at-risk groups.
• Wash raw produce, keep ready-to-eat foods separate and avoid long storage, because the bacteria grow in the refrigerator.
• Food industry controls and outbreak tracing.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: Cephalosporins do not cover Listeria: always add ampicillin to empirical meningitis therapy in neonates, older adults and the immunocompromised.
Rhombencephalitis with fever suggests Listeria.
Listeria grows in the refrigerator.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Tunkel AR et al. IDSA guidelines for bacterial meningitis. Clin Infect Dis 2004
Local public health food safety guidance

organisms.name: Bordetella pertussis
organisms.tagline: Highly contagious respiratory pathogen causing whooping cough, with prolonged paroxysmal cough; infants face the greatest risk of apnoea, pneumonia and death.
diseases: Apnoea and cyanosis in young infants
Prolonged cough in adolescents and adults

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Small, fastidious Gram-negative coccobacilli; strictly aerobic and non-motile.
• Needs special media: Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe charcoal agar; grows slowly (3 to 7 days).
• Oxidase-positive; infects only humans and attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium.
• B. parapertussis causes a milder similar illness.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi protein, raising cAMP; it causes lymphocytosis by blocking lymphocyte entry into tissues.
• Filamentous haemagglutinin, pertactin and fimbriae mediate adhesion to cilia.
• Adenylate cyclase toxin impairs phagocyte function.
• Tracheal cytotoxin damages ciliated cells and stops mucociliary clearance, causing the cough.
• Dermonecrotic toxin and lipooligosaccharide add local injury.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Humans are the only reservoir; spread by respiratory droplets, with a household attack rate of up to 80% in susceptible contacts.
• Epidemic peaks every 3 to 5 years, with resurgence in many countries because immunity from acellular vaccines wanes over several years.
• Adolescents and adults with mild or atypical disease are a major source for infants.
• Highest mortality in infants under 3 months, and in places with low vaccine coverage.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Catarrhal stage (1 to 2 weeks): coryza, mild cough and low-grade fever, when the patient is most infectious.
• Paroxysmal stage (2 to 6 weeks): bursts of rapid coughs followed by an inspiratory 'whoop', post-tussive vomiting, cyanosis and exhaustion, with the patient looking well between spells.
• Convalescent stage (weeks to months): gradual decline of cough.
• Infants may have apnoea, cyanosis or sudden death without a whoop.
• Marked lymphocytosis in infants suggests pertussis, and complications include pneumonia, seizures and encephalopathy.
• Adults: a cough lasting more than 2 weeks, often worse at night, with little fever.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab or aspirate is the preferred test in the first 3 weeks of cough.
• Culture on Regan-Lowe or Bordet-Gengou agar is specific but less sensitive, and needs early sampling.
• Serology (IgG to pertussis toxin) can help in late presentation in adolescents and adults.
• A full blood count showing high white cells with absolute lymphocytosis supports diagnosis in infants.
• Notify public health and trace close contacts.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• A macrolide is first-line: azithromycin (preferred in young infants) or clarithromycin; erythromycin carries a risk of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in newborns.
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the alternative for macrolide-intolerant patients older than 2 months.
• Antibiotics started in the catarrhal stage reduce symptoms; later they mainly stop spread.
• Supportive care: oxygen, hydration, feeding support and monitoring for apnoea; admit infants under 6 months.
• Cough suppressants, steroids and bronchodilators are not recommended.
• Isolate for at least 5 days of effective antibiotics, and give close contacts post-exposure antibiotics, especially if there are infants or pregnant women at home.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Macrolide-resistant strains (23S rRNA mutations) are common in China and reported elsewhere.
• Susceptibility testing is rarely done, so consider resistance with treatment failure.
• Pertactin-deficient strains have emerged under acellular vaccine pressure.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• DTaP in the childhood series, with a booster (Tdap) in adolescence.
• Tdap in every pregnancy (usually weeks 27 to 36) passes antibody to the newborn and is the best protection for infants.
• Household and healthcare worker vaccination, and post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts.
• Whole-cell vaccines cause more side effects but give longer protection and are still used in many countries.
• Natural infection and vaccine immunity both wane over time.

pearls: Adults with a cough over 2 weeks may be the source of infection for an infant.
Whoop is often absent in infants, so look for apnoea and cyanosis.
Antibiotics prevent spread, but only help symptoms if started early.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC Pink Book: Pertussis chapter
WHO position paper on pertussis vaccines

organisms.name: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
organisms.morphology: Club-shaped Gram-positive bacilli in 'Chinese letter' arrangements
organisms.tagline: Toxin-producing bacillus that causes respiratory diphtheria with an adherent pseudomembrane, plus myocarditis and neuropathy; vaccine-preventable but still causes outbreaks.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Club-shaped Gram-positive bacilli arranged in V and L shapes ('Chinese letters'); non-motile and non-spore-forming.
• Metachromatic (volutin) granules stain with Albert or Loeffler methylene blue.
• Grows on Loeffler serum slope and on tellurite media, producing black colonies on potassium tellurite agar.
• Only strains carrying the tox gene (a lysogenic beta-prophage) make toxin; biotypes include gravis, mitis, intermedius and belfanti.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Diphtheria toxin: an AB exotoxin whose B subunit binds the HB-EGF receptor, and whose A subunit ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (EF-2), blocking protein synthesis and killing cells.
• Toxin production is controlled by iron concentration, through the DtxR repressor.
• The toxin causes local necrosis that forms the pseudomembrane, and spreads in blood to heart, nerves and kidneys.
• Pili and other adhesins aid attachment to the throat.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Spread by respiratory droplets and by contact with skin lesions; humans are the main reservoir.
• Rare where vaccine coverage is high, but outbreaks occur when coverage falls (the former Soviet Union in the 1990s, and recent outbreaks in Yemen, Nigeria, Venezuela and Haiti).
• Adults with waning immunity, travellers and unvaccinated children are at risk.
• C. ulcerans, a zoonotic species carried by animals, can produce a diphtheria-like illness.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Incubation 2 to 5 days.
• Sore throat, low fever and malaise, then a grey, adherent pseudomembrane on the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds when scraped.
• 'Bull neck' from marked cervical lymphadenopathy and soft-tissue swelling, with foul breath.
• Laryngeal involvement causes stridor and airway obstruction.
• Myocarditis (typically at 1 to 2 weeks) causes arrhythmias and heart failure; neuropathy includes palatal palsy, cranial nerve palsies and later a peripheral polyneuropathy.
• Cutaneous diphtheria: a chronic non-healing punched-out ulcer with a grey membrane, common in tropical regions.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Suspect from the clinical picture and do not wait for the laboratory; alert the lab and public health.
• Swab from beneath the pseudomembrane for Gram stain, culture on Loeffler or tellurite media.
• Confirm toxin production by the Elek immunodiffusion test or PCR for the tox gene.
• ECG and troponin to monitor for myocarditis.
• Culture contacts and treat carriers.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Diphtheria antitoxin (equine) neutralizes circulating toxin and should be given as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, after hypersensitivity testing, because it cannot reverse toxin already bound in cells.
• Penicillin or a macrolide (erythromycin or azithromycin) is used to kill the organism and stop transmission.
• Airway management, including intubation or tracheostomy for obstruction; bed rest and cardiac monitoring.
• Respiratory droplet isolation until two negative cultures after antibiotics; contact precautions for cutaneous disease.
• Vaccinate recovering patients, since natural infection does not reliably give immunity.
• Close contacts: culture, antibiotic prophylaxis, booster vaccination, and surveillance for 7 days.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Generally susceptible to penicillin and macrolides.
• Reduced penicillin susceptibility and macrolide resistance have been reported in some regions, so check susceptibility.
• Resistance does not change the priority of antitoxin.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Diphtheria toxoid vaccine in DTaP or DTP (children) and Td or Tdap (adolescents and adults), with boosters every 10 years.
• High vaccine coverage prevents disease and limits circulation.
• Public health notification, contact tracing and outbreak response.
• Booster vaccination for travellers to endemic areas.

pearls: A grey adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds on scraping is classic for diphtheria.
Give antitoxin on clinical suspicion, without waiting for culture.
Diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A both inactivate EF-2 by ADP-ribosylation.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC Pink Book: Diphtheria chapter
WHO position paper on diphtheria vaccines

organisms.name: Bacillus anthracis
organisms.morphology: Large Gram-positive spore-forming bacilli in chains ('boxcar' appearance)
organisms.tagline: Spore-forming zoonotic bacillus causing anthrax: cutaneous disease with a black eschar, and life-threatening inhalational, gastrointestinal and injection forms.
diseases: Injection anthrax in people who inject drugs

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Large Gram-positive, aerobic, spore-forming bacilli, often in long chains with square ends ('boxcar' or 'bamboo' appearance); non-motile.
• Non-haemolytic, grey 'medusa head' colonies on blood agar, and tolerant of aerobic culture.
• Capsule is made of poly-D-glutamic acid, unusual among bacteria (it resists phagocytosis and is not a polysaccharide).
• Spores survive in soil for decades and resist heat, drying and many disinfectants.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Plasmid pXO1 encodes the tripartite toxin: protective antigen (PA) binds host receptors and forms a pore for the other two components.
• Edema factor (EF) is an adenylate cyclase that raises cAMP and causes oedema; lethal factor (LF) is a zinc metalloprotease that cleaves MAP kinase kinases and kills macrophages.
• Plasmid pXO2 encodes the poly-D-glutamic acid capsule.
• Spores are taken up by macrophages, germinate, and spread to lymph nodes, where bacteria multiply and release toxin.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• A zoonosis of herbivores (cattle, sheep, goats); humans are infected by contact with infected animals, hides, wool or meat, or by spore inhalation.
• Endemic in parts of Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Central and South America; sporadic in other regions.
• No sustained person-to-person spread.
• Anthrax is a notifiable disease and a recognized bioterrorism agent (the 2001 letter attacks in the United States, and the 1979 Sverdlovsk release).
• Injection anthrax has caused outbreaks among people who inject heroin in Europe.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Cutaneous (about 95% of natural cases): a painless papule that turns into a vesicle and then a black necrotic eschar with surrounding oedema; usually heals over weeks, but can become systemic.
• Inhalational: initial flu-like illness, then abrupt deterioration with respiratory failure, shock, widened mediastinum on chest X-ray and haemorrhagic pleural effusions, with high mortality.
• Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea after eating contaminated meat; oropharyngeal form with throat lesions.
• Injection: severe soft tissue infection at the injection site with systemic spread.
• Haemorrhagic meningitis can complicate any systemic form.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Gram stain and culture of blood, vesicle fluid, CSF, sputum or tissue; warn the laboratory because it is a select agent.
• Chest X-ray or CT showing mediastinal widening and pleural effusions supports inhalational anthrax.
• PCR, immunohistochemistry and toxin assays are done in reference laboratories.
• Treat on clinical suspicion, as delay is dangerous, and notify public health immediately.
• Anthrax meningitis: consider lumbar puncture only when safe.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Cutaneous anthrax: oral ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for about 7 to 10 days in naturally acquired disease, and 60 days if the exposure was to aerosolized spores.
• Systemic and inhalational anthrax: combination therapy with a bactericidal drug (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin, or meropenem) plus a protein-synthesis inhibitor (linezolid or clindamycin) to reduce toxin production.
• Antitoxins (raxibacumab, obiltoxaximab or anthrax immune globulin) are added for systemic disease.
• Meningitis: use regimens with good CSF penetration (ciprofloxacin or meropenem plus linezolid).
• Drain pleural effusions, and give intensive care support.
• Post-exposure prophylaxis: ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for 60 days, with vaccination.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Naturally susceptible to penicillin, but produces inducible beta-lactamases and cephalosporinases, so penicillin and cephalosporins are not used alone.
• Intrinsically resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and many cephalosporins.
• Fluoroquinolones, doxycycline, linezolid, clindamycin and carbapenems remain active.
• Engineered resistant strains are a bioterrorism concern.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Vaccination of animals in endemic regions, and safe disposal of carcasses (do not open them).
• Anthrax vaccine adsorbed (AVA, BioThrax) and the newer Cyfendus are used for at-risk workers and for post-exposure use.
• Protection of laboratory and veterinary workers; processing controls for imported hides and wool.
• Public health tracing and decontamination after exposures.

pearls: Painless black eschar with surrounding oedema: think cutaneous anthrax.
Inhalational anthrax shows a widened mediastinum, not pneumonia infiltrates.
Capsule of poly-D-glutamic acid is unique among bacteria.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC clinical guidance on anthrax (current version)
WHO guidance on anthrax in humans and animals

organisms.name: Campylobacter jejuni
organisms.morphology: Curved, spiral Gram-negative bacilli (comma or gull-wing shape), microaerophilic
organisms.tagline: Leading bacterial cause of infectious diarrhoea worldwide, usually from undercooked poultry, with Guillain-Barre syndrome as its best-known complication.
diseases: Guillain-Barre syndrome and Miller Fisher syndrome

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Slender, curved or S-shaped Gram-negative rods with a single polar flagellum and darting 'corkscrew' motility.
• Microaerophilic: needs low oxygen and raised carbon dioxide, so it will not grow in routine aerobic conditions.
• Grows best at 42 degrees Celsius on selective media (Skirrow or CCDA agar), which helps separate it from other enteric pathogens.
• Oxidase-positive and catalase-positive; C. jejuni hydrolyses hippurate.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Flagella give motility through intestinal mucus and aid colonization.
• Cytolethal distending toxin (CDT) causes DNA damage and cell cycle arrest.
• Invasion of the intestinal epithelium, mostly in the jejunum, ileum and colon, causes inflammatory diarrhoea.
• Lipooligosaccharide mimics human gangliosides (GM1 and GQ1b), which triggers autoantibodies that cause Guillain-Barre syndrome.
• Surface capsule and surface glycans help evade immunity.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• One of the commonest causes of bacterial gastroenteritis in high-income and low-income countries.
• Reservoir is the gut of poultry and other animals; transmission is by undercooked chicken, cross-contamination in the kitchen, unpasteurized milk, untreated water and contact with pets or farm animals.
• Peaks in children under 5 and young adults, with a summer seasonal peak in temperate regions.
• Low infectious dose (about 500 organisms); outbreaks are less common than sporadic cases.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Incubation 2 to 5 days.
• Fever, malaise and headache, then crampy abdominal pain and diarrhoea that may be watery or bloody; usually resolves in about a week.
• Abdominal pain can mimic acute appendicitis.
• Guillain-Barre syndrome follows roughly 1 in 1,000 infections, 1 to 3 weeks later: ascending weakness with areflexia.
• Reactive arthritis may follow 1 to 3 weeks later, particularly in HLA-B27-positive people.
• Bacteraemia and invasive disease occur in older adults, immunocompromised hosts and those with hypogammaglobulinaemia.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Stool culture on selective agar in a microaerophilic atmosphere at 42 degrees Celsius.
• Multiplex PCR panels and antigen tests detect Campylobacter quickly and are widely used.
• Ask the laboratory to include Campylobacter on the request for bloody or prolonged diarrhoea.
• Gram stain of stool showing curved bacilli with many white cells supports the diagnosis.
• Blood cultures if the patient is septic or immunocompromised.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Most cases are self-limited, and rehydration is the main treatment.
• Antibiotics are reserved for severe illness, high fever, bloody stools, prolonged symptoms, pregnancy and immunocompromised patients.
• Azithromycin is the preferred drug.
• Fluoroquinolones are no longer reliable because of high resistance in many regions.
• Avoid antimotility agents when diarrhoea is bloody or the patient is febrile.
• Guillain-Barre syndrome needs supportive care, with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; antibiotics do not prevent or treat it.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Fluoroquinolone resistance (gyrA mutation) is very common, often above 50% in parts of Asia and Europe.
• Macrolide resistance is still low but rising (23S rRNA and erm(B)), and is higher in C. coli.
• Tetracycline resistance is common.
• Check local susceptibility data before choosing therapy.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Cook poultry thoroughly, and avoid cross-contamination of cutting boards, hands and ready-to-eat foods.
• Drink pasteurized milk and treated water.
• Handwashing after contact with animals and raw meat.
• Farm-level biosecurity and processing controls reduce poultry contamination.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: Think Campylobacter when diarrhoea follows undercooked chicken.
Campylobacter is the commonest antecedent infection of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Fluoroquinolones are no longer first-line because of resistance.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Shane AL et al. IDSA guidelines for infectious diarrhoea. Clin Infect Dis 2017
Local antimicrobial guidelines and susceptibility data

organisms.name: Helicobacter pylori
organisms.morphology: Curved Gram-negative spiral bacilli, microaerophilic, urease-positive
organisms.tagline: Gastric pathogen colonizing about half of the world's population; the main cause of peptic ulcer disease and a recognized carcinogen for gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
diseases: Iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia (association)

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Curved or spiral Gram-negative rods with multiple polar flagella; microaerophilic.
• Strongly urease-positive, plus oxidase-positive and catalase-positive.
• Slow-growing, fastidious organism cultured on selective media for 3 to 7 days in a microaerophilic atmosphere.
• Lives in the mucus layer of the stomach, next to the epithelium.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, buffering gastric acid around the bacterium.
• Flagella provide motility through the gastric mucus; adhesins (BabA, SabA) bind gastric epithelial cells.
• The cag pathogenicity island encodes a type IV secretion system that injects CagA into epithelial cells, driving inflammation and carcinogenesis.
• Vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA) forms pores and causes vacuolation and cell death.
• Chronic infection causes persistent inflammation of the mucosa.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Infects roughly 40 to 50% of people worldwide, with higher rates in low-income regions.
• Usually acquired in childhood, by oral-oral or faecal-oral routes within families; once acquired it persists for life unless treated.
• Prevalence is falling in high-income countries.
• Gastric cancer risk is greatest in East Asia, parts of Eastern Europe and Latin America.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Most infected people have no symptoms.
• Duodenal ulcer (antral-predominant gastritis with high acid): epigastric pain that is often relieved by food, and often worse at night.
• Gastric ulcer and cancer (corpus-predominant gastritis with low acid): pain that may be worse with eating, weight loss, early satiety.
• Complications: bleeding, perforation and gastric outlet obstruction.
• Alarm features needing endoscopy: age over 50 to 60 with new dyspepsia, weight loss, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, anaemia or GI bleeding.
• H. pylori is associated with iron deficiency anaemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Non-invasive tests: urea breath test or stool antigen test, which detect active infection and are used to confirm eradication.
• Stop proton pump inhibitors for 2 weeks and antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks before breath or stool testing, to avoid false negatives.
• At endoscopy: rapid urease test, histology and culture; culture with susceptibility is useful after treatment failure.
• Serology only shows past exposure, so it cannot confirm current infection or cure; use it only where other tests are not available and the pre-test probability is high.
• Test and treat patients with peptic ulcer, MALT lymphoma, and selected dyspepsia.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• First-line in most regions: bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days (a proton pump inhibitor, bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole).
• Clarithromycin-based triple therapy only if local clarithromycin resistance is known to be low (under 15%) or susceptibility is confirmed.
• Other options: rifabutin-based, or potassium-competitive acid blocker (vonoprazan) regimens, where available.
• Penicillin allergy: bismuth quadruple therapy is preferred.
• Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after finishing treatment, and at least 2 weeks after stopping a proton pump inhibitor.
• Eradication heals ulcers and lowers ulcer recurrence and gastric cancer risk, and can cause remission of low-grade MALT lymphoma.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Clarithromycin resistance (23S rRNA mutations) is the main driver of treatment failure and is common worldwide.
• Metronidazole resistance is also frequent (rdxA and frxA mutations), but is partly overcome by higher doses and longer courses.
• Levofloxacin resistance (gyrA) limits fluoroquinolone-based regimens.
• Amoxicillin and tetracycline resistance remain rare.
• Previous macrolide exposure predicts clarithromycin resistance.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• No vaccine is available.
• Screen-and-treat programmes are used in some high-risk regions for gastric cancer prevention.
• Test and treat first-degree relatives of gastric cancer patients and other high-risk groups.
• Improved sanitation and living conditions reduce transmission.

pearls: Urease-positive curved bacilli in the stomach: H. pylori.
Stop PPIs for 2 weeks before a breath or stool test to avoid false negatives.
Always confirm eradication after treatment, because resistance is common.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
ACG clinical guideline on treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection (current version)
Maastricht VI/Florence consensus report on H. pylori management

organisms.name: Shigella species
organisms.tagline: Highly infectious cause of bacillary dysentery with a very low infectious dose; spreads by the faecal-oral route and drives outbreaks in crowded settings and in children in low-income regions.
diseases: Febrile seizures and encephalopathy in children

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative, non-motile bacilli and facultative anaerobes.
• Non-lactose fermenter: colourless colonies on MacConkey agar, and no H2S production on XLD or Salmonella-Shigella agar (unlike Salmonella).
• Four species: S. dysenteriae (group A), S. flexneri (B), S. boydii (C) and S. sonnei (D).
• Very closely related to E. coli, and enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) causes an almost identical disease.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• The invasion plasmid encodes a type III secretion system (Ipa proteins) that lets the bacteria invade colonic epithelial cells through M cells.
• IcsA drives actin-based motility, spreading the bacteria from cell to cell and escaping immune detection.
• Shiga toxin (S. dysenteriae type 1) inactivates the 60S ribosomal subunit (it removes an adenine from 28S rRNA), causing cell death and HUS.
• Shigella enterotoxins contribute to early watery diarrhoea.
• Survives gastric acid, so as few as 10 to 100 organisms can cause disease.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Spread by the faecal-oral route: person-to-person, food, water and flies; humans and some primates are the only reservoir.
• S. sonnei predominates in high-income countries; S. flexneri is more frequent in low-income countries; S. dysenteriae type 1 causes epidemics in crowded or disaster-affected regions.
• Outbreaks in day-care centres, institutions, refugee camps, and among men who have sex with men.
• Major cause of diarrhoeal death in children under 5 in low-income regions, linked to stunting.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Incubation 1 to 3 days.
• Fever, cramping abdominal pain, tenesmus and watery diarrhoea that may progress to dysentery with small-volume bloody, mucoid stools.
• Children can have febrile seizures; most cases resolve within 5 to 7 days.
• HUS follows S. dysenteriae type 1 infection, causing haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and kidney injury.
• Reactive arthritis (with urethritis and conjunctivitis) in HLA-B27-positive adults.
• Complications are more frequent in malnourished and immunocompromised patients.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Stool culture on MacConkey, XLD or Hektoen agar; microscopy shows many neutrophils and red cells.
• Multiplex PCR panels are widely used and detect Shigella and EIEC (the two are not distinguished by many assays).
• Susceptibility testing is important because of increasing resistance.
• Blood cultures if the patient is septic, malnourished or immunocompromised.
• Notify public health authorities.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Oral or intravenous rehydration is the key treatment; zinc supplementation for children in low-income regions.
• Antibiotics shorten illness and reduce shedding in moderate to severe disease, dysentery, and in vulnerable patients.
• Options: azithromycin, ciprofloxacin or another fluoroquinolone, or ceftriaxone, chosen by local susceptibility.
• Avoid antimotility drugs because they can prolong illness and increase complications.
• In S. dysenteriae type 1, antibiotics may increase HUS risk theoretically, but effective treatment is still advised; supportive care for HUS.
• Exclude infected people from food handling, childcare and healthcare work until they are cleared.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Resistance to ampicillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and tetracycline is widespread.
• Fluoroquinolone resistance (gyrA and parC mutations) is increasing, and is reported in many regions.
• ESBL production and azithromycin resistance (mphA, ermB) occur.
• Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Shigella, especially in men who have sex with men, is a growing concern.
• Culture and susceptibility testing is needed to guide treatment.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Handwashing with soap, safe drinking water, sanitation and food hygiene.
• Exclusion of infected children from day-care until recovered.
• Outbreak investigation, and partner treatment and counselling for sexually transmitted cases.
• No licensed vaccine is available, although several candidates are in trials.

pearls: Only 10 to 100 organisms can cause shigellosis.
Shiga toxin from S. dysenteriae type 1 can cause HUS, as can EHEC.
Avoid antimotility drugs in dysentery.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Shane AL et al. IDSA guidelines for infectious diarrhoea. Clin Infect Dis 2017
WHO guidelines for the control of shigellosis

organisms.name: Bacteroides fragilis
organisms.tagline: Dominant anaerobe of the gut and the commonest anaerobe in intra-abdominal and pelvic abscesses; infection follows spillage of bowel contents and needs drainage as well as antibiotics.
diseases: Diabetic foot and decubitus ulcer infection
Brain abscess (from contiguous or metastatic spread)

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Pleomorphic Gram-negative bacilli that stain faintly and are strictly anaerobic.
• Bile-tolerant: grows on Bacteroides bile esculin (BBE) agar, and hydrolyses esculin.
• Usually resistant to kanamycin, vancomycin and colistin special-potency disks, which helps with identification.
• Identified now by MALDI-TOF; makes up the largest group of anaerobes in the colon.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Polysaccharide capsule (PSA) triggers T-cell mediated abscess formation, which is unusual for a polysaccharide antigen.
• The lipopolysaccharide is weakly endotoxic compared with that of Enterobacterales.
• Superoxide dismutase and catalase give limited aerotolerance, allowing survival in tissues.
• Enterotoxigenic strains produce B. fragilis toxin (fragilysin), a metalloprotease linked to diarrhoea and possibly colorectal cancer.
• Beta-lactamases and efflux pumps protect it from antibiotics; adherence factors and fimbriae aid colonization.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Part of the normal flora of the colon, where anaerobes outnumber aerobes by about 1,000 to 1.
• Infection follows breach of the mucosa by surgery, trauma, perforation, ischaemia or malignancy.
• Usually polymicrobial with enteric Gram-negative bacilli and enterococci.
• Anaerobic infection below the diaphragm is typically Bacteroides, and above the diaphragm it is typically Prevotella, Fusobacterium and Peptostreptococcus.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Abdominal pain, fever and leucocytosis; localized abscess or generalized peritonitis after perforation.
• Foul-smelling pus and gas formation are clues to anaerobic infection.
• Pelvic infections: post-partum endometritis and tubo-ovarian abscess.
• Liver abscess, usually from biliary or portal spread.
• Bacteraemia often arises from an abdominal source and carries high mortality when untreated.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Imaging by ultrasound or CT shows collections and gas.
• Collect pus or tissue (not swabs) and transport anaerobically; Gram stain may show mixed flora and Gram-negative bacilli.
• Anaerobic culture on blood agar and BBE agar, and MALDI-TOF for identification.
• Blood cultures with anaerobic bottles.
• Susceptibility testing is not routine but is useful in serious or recurrent infection.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Source control is essential: drain abscesses, debride necrotic tissue and repair perforations.
• Metronidazole is the most reliable anaerobic agent and is used with cover for enteric Gram-negative bacilli.
• Beta-lactam with beta-lactamase inhibitor (piperacillin-tazobactam, or amoxicillin-clavulanate for milder disease), or a carbapenem for severe infection.
• Moxifloxacin is an alternative, but resistance is common.
• Clindamycin is no longer reliable because of high resistance.
• Aminoglycosides, aztreonam and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole have no anaerobic activity.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Almost all strains produce beta-lactamases (cepA), so penicillin and ampicillin fail.
• Carbapenem resistance by the cfiA metallo-beta-lactamase gene is uncommon but important.
• Clindamycin resistance (erm genes) is frequent, and moxifloxacin resistance is increasing.
• Metronidazole resistance (nim genes) is rare.
• Intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides, because uptake needs oxygen.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Timely source control and surgical care.
• Perioperative prophylaxis for colorectal surgery covers anaerobes with a cephalosporin plus metronidazole, or another regimen.
• Good surgical technique and appropriate antibiotics for perforated viscus.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: Anaerobes below the diaphragm: Bacteroides; above: Prevotella and Fusobacterium.
Aminoglycosides do not work against anaerobes.
Foul smell and gas in pus suggest anaerobic infection.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Solomkin JS et al. IDSA/SIS guidelines for complicated intra-abdominal infection
Local antimicrobial guidelines and susceptibility data

organisms.name: Borrelia burgdorferi
organisms.morphology: Loosely coiled, microaerophilic spirochete (too thin for Gram stain)
organisms.tagline: Tick-borne spirochete causing Lyme disease: erythema migrans, then early disseminated nervous system and heart involvement, and late arthritis.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Loosely coiled spirochete with periplasmic flagella; microaerophilic and slow-growing.
• Grows in Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly (BSK) medium, but culture is not used for routine diagnosis.
• Seen in tissue with silver stain or dark-field microscopy, and stains poorly with Gram stain.
• Species complex: B. burgdorferi (North America and Europe), B. afzelii and B. garinii (Europe and Asia).

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• OspA binds the tick gut; OspC is upregulated after the tick feeds and aids transmission to the host.
• VlsE undergoes antigenic variation to escape antibody.
• Complement regulator-acquiring surface proteins (such as CRASP) bind factor H to avoid complement killing.
• Adhesins (DbpA, BBK32) bind decorin and fibronectin, aiding spread through tissues.
• No classic toxins: damage arises mainly from the inflammatory response to lipoproteins.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Transmitted by Ixodes ticks (I. scapularis and I. pacificus in North America, I. ricinus in Europe, I. persulcatus in Asia); the tick must usually be attached for 36 hours or more.
• White-footed mice and other small mammals are the reservoir, and deer feed the adult ticks.
• Most common vector-borne disease in the United States and Europe, with cases peaking in late spring and summer.
• The same tick can transmit Anaplasma, Babesia and Powassan virus (co-infection).
• Relapsing fever Borrelia (B. recurrentis by lice; B. hermsii by soft ticks) are different species.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Early localized (3 to 30 days): erythema migrans, an expanding red annular rash, often with central clearing ('bull's-eye'), with fever, myalgia and fatigue.
• Early disseminated (weeks to months): multiple erythema migrans lesions, facial nerve palsy (often bilateral), lymphocytic meningitis, radiculoneuritis and carditis with AV block.
• Late (months to years): oligoarticular arthritis of large joints, especially the knee; acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans in Europe; late neurological disease is rare.
• Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome: persistent fatigue and pain after treatment, without evidence of ongoing infection.
• Most patients do not recall a tick bite.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Erythema migrans in an endemic area is diagnosed clinically; do not wait for serology.
• Two-tier serology (an enzyme immunoassay followed by IgM and IgG immunoblot, or a modified two-tier with two EIAs) is used for suspected disseminated disease.
• Antibodies take 2 to 6 weeks to appear, so early serology is often negative.
• Do not test asymptomatic people or those with non-specific symptoms: positive tests may reflect old infection.
• Neuroborreliosis: CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis and intrathecal antibody; PCR of joint fluid in arthritis; ECG when carditis is suspected.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Erythema migrans: doxycycline for 10 days; amoxicillin or cefuroxime axetil for 14 days when doxycycline is not suitable (for example in pregnancy and breastfeeding).
• Facial palsy alone: oral doxycycline; meningitis and radiculitis: doxycycline or intravenous ceftriaxone.
• Carditis with high-grade AV block: intravenous ceftriaxone with cardiac monitoring, then oral therapy.
• Arthritis: oral antibiotic for 28 days; persistent synovitis may need a second course or anti-inflammatory therapy.
• Prolonged or repeated antibiotic courses do not help post-treatment symptoms.
• A single dose of doxycycline within 72 hours of a high-risk Ixodes bite in an endemic area can prevent disease.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• No clinically meaningful acquired resistance to doxycycline, amoxicillin or ceftriaxone.
• Macrolides such as azithromycin are less effective and not first-line.
• First-generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones and clindamycin should not be used for treatment.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Avoid tick habitats, wear long clothing, use repellents (DEET or permethrin-treated clothing), and check for ticks after outdoor exposure.
• Remove attached ticks promptly with fine tweezers; removal within 24 hours makes transmission unlikely.
• Post-exposure doxycycline for selected high-risk bites, as above.
• A human Lyme vaccine is not currently available for routine use; trials of a new vaccine are ongoing.
• Landscape and rodent management help reduce risk.

pearls: Treat erythema migrans clinically; early serology is often negative.
Bilateral facial palsy in an endemic area: think Lyme disease.
Lyme carditis can cause complete heart block in young people.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
IDSA/AAN/ACR guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of Lyme disease (2020)
CDC clinical guidance on Lyme disease

organisms.name: Rickettsia species
organisms.tagline: Arthropod-borne obligate intracellular bacteria that infect vascular endothelium, causing spotted fever and typhus group diseases such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever; early doxycycline saves lives.
diseases: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi, a related genus)

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Small obligate intracellular Gram-negative coccobacilli that cannot grow on routine media.
• Stain poorly with Gram stain; seen with Giemsa, Gimenez or Machiavello stains or by immunofluorescence.
• Cultured only in cell lines or animals in reference laboratories.
• Divided into the spotted fever group and the typhus group; Orientia (scrub typhus) is placed in a separate genus.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Surface proteins OmpA and OmpB mediate adhesion to and entry into endothelial cells.
• Phospholipase and haemolysin allow escape from the phagosome into the cytoplasm.
• Actin-based motility (RickA and Sca2) spreads the bacteria from cell to cell in spotted fever group species.
• Infection of vascular endothelial cells causes widespread vasculitis, increased vascular permeability, oedema and microvascular thrombosis.
• Lipopolysaccharide and oxidative injury add to the damage.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Spotted fever group is spread by ticks (R. rickettsii by Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus ticks), epidemic typhus by body lice, murine typhus by rat fleas, rickettsialpox by mites and scrub typhus by chiggers.
• Rocky Mountain spotted fever occurs across the Americas, mostly in spring and summer, and is most common in the south-eastern and south-central United States.
• Untreated Rocky Mountain spotted fever has a case-fatality of about 20 to 25%, and delayed treatment raises mortality.
• Epidemic typhus occurs with crowding, war and poor hygiene; scrub typhus is endemic across the 'tsutsugamushi triangle' of Asia and the Pacific.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Incubation about 3 to 12 days after a tick bite (many patients do not recall one).
• Sudden fever, severe headache, myalgia, nausea and vomiting.
• Rash appears 2 to 5 days after the fever starts: macules at the wrists and ankles that spread centripetally to the trunk and involve the palms and soles, becoming petechial; the rash is absent in a minority of patients.
• Severe disease: confusion, seizures, shock, pulmonary and renal failure, gangrene of the digits, hyponatraemia, thrombocytopenia and raised liver enzymes.
• Scrub typhus: an eschar at the bite site, regional lymphadenopathy and rash.
• Murine typhus: fever, headache and a truncal rash after flea exposure.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Diagnosis is clinical in the first days: treat on suspicion and do not wait for laboratory results.
• PCR of a skin biopsy of a rash lesion or of blood is the best early test, although blood PCR is less sensitive early on.
• Serology (indirect immunofluorescence) rises only after 7 to 10 days, so paired acute and convalescent samples are used for confirmation.
• Typical laboratory findings: thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia, mildly raised transaminases and normal or low white cell count.
• Weil-Felix is obsolete because it is insensitive and non-specific.
• Report to public health authorities.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for all ages, including children and, for severe disease, pregnancy; start immediately on suspicion.
• Continue until the patient has been afebrile for at least 3 days, with a minimum course of 5 to 7 days.
• Delay of treatment beyond the fifth day of illness greatly raises the risk of death.
• Chloramphenicol is an alternative only when doxycycline cannot be used, but it is linked to worse outcomes.
• Scrub typhus and murine typhus: doxycycline, with azithromycin as an alternative (for example in pregnancy and children, per guidance).
• Supportive care in intensive care units for shock, respiratory and renal failure.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, macrolides (except some newer ones) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
• Sulfonamides can worsen the course of Rocky Mountain spotted fever and should be avoided.
• Fluoroquinolones have some activity but are less effective than doxycycline.
• Acquired resistance to doxycycline has not been shown in practice, though reduced susceptibility has been reported in some Orientia strains.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Avoid tick habitats, wear protective clothing, use repellents and permethrin-treated clothing, and perform tick checks, removing ticks quickly.
• Control of body lice (hygiene, delousing, clothing treatment) for epidemic typhus; rodent and flea control for murine typhus.
• Doxycycline prophylaxis after a tick bite is not recommended for Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
• No licensed vaccine is available.
• Treat dogs and the environment for ticks in endemic areas.

pearls: Fever, headache and a rash that starts on the wrists and ankles: start doxycycline immediately.
Do not wait for a test: early serology is negative.
Avoid sulfonamides in suspected rickettsial infection, and use doxycycline even in children.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC clinical guidance on tickborne rickettsial diseases (Biggs HM et al. MMWR 2016)
WHO guidance on rickettsial diseases

organisms.name: Mycobacterium leprae
organisms.morphology: Acid-fast bacilli, obligate intracellular, cannot be cultured in vitro
organisms.tagline: Slow-growing intracellular bacillus causing leprosy (Hansen disease), a chronic infection of skin and peripheral nerves whose spectrum depends on the host's cell-mediated immunity.
diseases: Peripheral neuropathy with deformity and disability

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Acid-fast bacilli, stained with Ziehl-Neelsen or the modified Fite-Faraco method (weaker decolorizer); often seen in clumps called globi.
• Obligate intracellular organism that cannot be grown on artificial media; grown in mouse footpads and nine-banded armadillos.
• Very slow dividing (about 12 to 14 days per generation), with an optimal growth temperature of about 30 degrees Celsius.
• Prefers cooler body sites: skin, peripheral nerves, nasal mucosa, and testes.
• M. lepromatosis is a closely related species that also causes leprosy.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Phenolic glycolipid-1 (PGL-1) binds laminin in the Schwann cell basal lamina, which explains the tropism for peripheral nerves.
• Invades and survives within macrophages and Schwann cells.
• The cell wall mycolic acid layer protects the organism from host defences.
• Most tissue damage comes from the host immune response, not from toxins.
• Reduced cell-mediated immunity to M. leprae allows many bacilli to multiply (lepromatous form).

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Transmitted by prolonged close contact, probably through nasal droplets from untreated multibacillary patients.
• India, Brazil and Indonesia account for most new cases worldwide.
• Incubation is long: usually 2 to 10 years, and sometimes longer.
• Zoonotic reservoirs exist: armadillos in the southern United States, and red squirrels in parts of the British Isles.
• Most people have natural immunity, and household contacts of patients are at higher risk.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Tuberculoid (strong Th1 response): few, well-defined hypopigmented, anaesthetic skin patches with thickened nerves; few or no bacilli.
• Lepromatous (weak cell-mediated response): many symmetric nodules and plaques, diffuse skin thickening ('leonine facies'), loss of eyebrows, nasal collapse, and many bacilli.
• Borderline forms lie between these two poles and can shift (downgrade or upgrade) over time.
• Nerve damage: loss of sensation, muscle weakness, claw hand, foot drop and trophic ulcers; commonly affects the ulnar, median, common peroneal, posterior tibial and great auricular nerves.
• Type 1 (reversal) reaction: sudden inflammation of existing lesions and nerves with risk of permanent nerve damage.
• Type 2 reaction (erythema nodosum leprosum): painful nodules, fever, arthritis, neuritis and uveitis from immune complexes, mostly in lepromatous disease.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Clinical diagnosis: a hypopigmented or reddish skin patch with definite sensory loss, a thickened peripheral nerve, or acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear.
• Slit-skin smear and skin biopsy show acid-fast bacilli, granulomas and nerve involvement, and define the type and bacterial index.
• PCR can confirm the diagnosis and helps in difficult cases.
• Check for nerve function (sensation and muscle strength) at baseline and during follow-up.
• Lepromin skin test has no diagnostic value now.
• Examine household contacts, and report cases to public health authorities.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• WHO recommends multidrug therapy (MDT) with rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine, never a single drug.
• Paucibacillary leprosy: 6 months of MDT; multibacillary leprosy: 12 months of MDT.
• Treatment is usually given free of charge through national programmes, and makes patients non-infectious quickly.
• Reactions need prompt treatment: corticosteroids for type 1 reactions and neuritis; corticosteroids, clofazimine or thalidomide for type 2 reactions (thalidomide is strictly contraindicated in pregnancy because of teratogenicity).
• Continue MDT during a reaction; rehabilitation, footwear and self-care prevent disability.
• Follow up for relapse and for nerve damage after completing treatment.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Dapsone resistance (folP1 mutations), rifampicin resistance (rpoB mutations) and fluoroquinolone resistance (gyrA mutations) have been documented, but remain uncommon.
• Resistance is mainly seen after dapsone monotherapy and in relapses; molecular testing is available in reference laboratories.
• Second-line options include fluoroquinolones, minocycline, clarithromycin and bedaquiline, selected by specialists.
• Drug resistance is monitored through national surveillance.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Early detection and treatment of cases stops transmission.
• Contact tracing and a single dose of rifampicin as post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts is recommended by WHO.
• BCG vaccination gives partial protection.
• Prevent disability through early nerve function checks, self-care education and rehabilitation.
• Reduce stigma by educating communities that leprosy is curable, and that treated patients are not infectious.

pearls: Hypopigmented anaesthetic skin patch plus a thickened nerve is leprosy until proven otherwise.
Lepromatous leprosy has a weak Th2 response and many bacilli; tuberculoid leprosy has a strong Th1 response and few bacilli.
M. leprae grows best in cool areas: skin, nerves, nose and testes (also armadillo footpads).
Never treat leprosy with a single drug.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
WHO guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy
Local national leprosy programme guidance

organisms.name: Mycobacterium avium complex
organisms.tagline: Environmental nontuberculous mycobacteria that cause chronic lung disease in structurally damaged lungs, disseminated infection in advanced HIV, and lymphadenitis in children.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Acid-fast bacilli; slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) that take 2 to 6 weeks to grow in culture.
• Includes M. avium, M. intracellulare and M. chimaera; non-pigmented or slightly yellow colonies.
• Found in soil, natural and municipal water, biofilms, shower heads and hot tubs.
• Distinguished from M. tuberculosis by molecular methods, MALDI-TOF or sequencing.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• The lipid-rich cell wall resists chlorine and many disinfectants, and allows biofilm formation in water systems.
• Survives and replicates inside macrophages by blocking phagosome maturation.
• Glycopeptidolipids affect colony morphology and virulence.
• Disease depends mostly on host susceptibility: structural lung disease, or impaired cell-mediated immunity (such as low CD4 count or defects in the interferon-gamma/IL-12 pathway).

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• The most common nontuberculous mycobacteria causing lung disease in many regions, with rising incidence.
• Acquired from the environment (inhalation or ingestion); not spread between people, and not notifiable in most places.
• Pulmonary disease: older, often thin, non-smoking women with bronchiectasis (nodular form), and smokers or people with COPD (cavitary form).
• Disseminated disease: HIV with CD4 count below 50 cells per microlitre.
• M. chimaera infections have been linked to contaminated heater-cooler units used in cardiac surgery.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Pulmonary: chronic cough, fatigue, weight loss, sputum and sometimes haemoptysis, progressing over months to years.
• Nodular bronchiectatic form: nodules and bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe and lingula ('Lady Windermere syndrome').
• Fibrocavitary form: upper-lobe cavities, looking like tuberculosis and progressing faster.
• Disseminated: fever, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhoea, anaemia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and raised alkaline phosphatase.
• Hypersensitivity pneumonitis after hot tub exposure.
• Children: unilateral, painless submandibular or cervical lymph node enlargement.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Pulmonary MAC needs symptoms, compatible radiology (CT) and microbiological confirmation: at least two positive sputum cultures, or one positive bronchoalveolar lavage or lung biopsy culture.
• Acid-fast smear and culture, with species identification; blood cultures in suspected disseminated disease (mycobacterial blood culture).
• A single positive sputum culture does not prove disease, because the organism is found in the environment.
• Rule out tuberculosis, and screen for HIV and other immune defects.
• Susceptibility testing to macrolides and amikacin is recommended.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Pulmonary MAC: a three-drug regimen of a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin), rifampin and ethambutol.
• Nodular bronchiectatic disease usually receives the regimen three times weekly; cavitary or severe disease receives it daily, with amikacin (intravenous or inhaled liposomal) added.
• Treat until sputum cultures are negative for 12 months.
• Never use macrolide monotherapy, because resistance emerges quickly.
• Disseminated MAC in HIV: a macrolide plus ethambutol, with rifabutin sometimes added, and start antiretroviral therapy.
• Children with lymphadenitis are best managed by complete surgical excision.
• Chronic lung disease patients need airway clearance and long-term specialist follow-up.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Resistant to the standard first-line tuberculosis drugs isoniazid and pyrazinamide.
• Macrolide resistance is the main cause of treatment failure, through 23S rRNA (rrl) gene mutations, often after macrolide monotherapy or poor adherence.
• Amikacin resistance (rrs mutations) occurs with prolonged aminoglycoside use.
• In vitro susceptibility is not well correlated with outcome for drugs other than macrolides and amikacin.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• In HIV, early antiretroviral therapy prevents disseminated MAC; azithromycin prophylaxis is only considered if CD4 is below 50 and ART is not started immediately.
• Avoid contaminated water in at-risk patients: clean shower heads, humidifiers and hot tubs.
• Hospital water system and heater-cooler unit controls in cardiac surgery.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: Never use macrolide monotherapy for MAC.
A single positive sputum culture does not prove disease.
Lady Windermere syndrome: older thin woman with bronchiectasis in the right middle lobe and lingula.
Disseminated MAC in HIV is a CD4-below-50 infection.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Daley CL et al. ATS/ERS/ESCMID/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease. Clin Infect Dis 2020
Guidelines for the prevention and treatment of opportunistic infections in adults with HIV (NIH/CDC/IDSA)

organisms.name: Nocardia species
organisms.morphology: Gram-positive, beaded, branching filamentous bacilli (weakly acid-fast)
organisms.tagline: Aerobic soil actinomycete causing pulmonary, brain and cutaneous infection, mostly in patients with impaired T-cell immunity; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the backbone of treatment.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive, thin, beaded, branching filamentous rods that fragment into bacillary forms.
• Weakly (partially) acid-fast: it stains with a modified Kinyoun stain using a weak acid decolorizer, but not with the standard Ziehl-Neelsen method.
• Strictly aerobic and catalase-positive; grows slowly (up to 2 weeks) on routine media, with dry, chalky white colonies and an earthy smell.
• Main species: N. asteroides complex, N. cyriacigeorgica, N. farcinica, N. nova and N. brasiliensis (the latter is a common cause of skin infection).
• Not to be confused with Actinomyces (anaerobic, not acid-fast, with sulfur granules).

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Resists phagocytosis and survives within macrophages by blocking phagosome-lysosome fusion.
• Cell wall components (such as trehalose dimycolate, a cord-factor analogue) delay killing.
• Catalase and superoxide dismutase protect against oxidative killing.
• Tends to form abscesses with suppuration and necrosis, and can spread by blood to the brain, skin and other organs.
• Cell-mediated immunity is key to defence, so T-cell defects greatly increase risk.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Found worldwide in soil, decaying vegetation and water.
• Acquired by inhalation of dust or by direct inoculation through skin trauma; not spread between people.
• Risk factors: long-term corticosteroids, solid organ and haematopoietic cell transplant, HIV, malignancy, TNF inhibitors, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis and chronic lung disease.
• About a third of cases occur in people without recognized immunosuppression, particularly cutaneous disease.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Pulmonary: subacute cough, fever, dyspnoea and weight loss, with nodules, consolidation, cavities and pleural effusion; resembles tuberculosis, fungal infection or malignancy.
• Brain abscess in about a quarter of disseminated cases, often single or multiple, with subtle symptoms.
• Skin: nodules and ulcers, and lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) spread after trauma, particularly with N. brasiliensis.
• Mycetoma: chronic swelling, draining sinuses and grains.
• Disseminated disease may involve skin, bone, eyes and kidneys.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Gram stain and modified acid-fast stain of sputum, pus or tissue showing beaded branching rods.
• Culture on routine or selective (buffered charcoal yeast extract) media for up to 2 weeks; warn the laboratory, because plates are often discarded too early.
• Species identification by MALDI-TOF or sequencing, and susceptibility testing by a reference laboratory.
• MRI or CT of the brain in all patients with pulmonary or disseminated nocardiosis.
• Biopsy or aspiration of abscesses when possible.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the first-line agent.
• Severe, disseminated or central nervous system disease: combination therapy with TMP-SMX plus imipenem, amikacin, or linezolid, based on susceptibility.
• Surgical drainage of abscesses has an important role.
• Duration: at least 6 months for pulmonary and cutaneous disease in immunocompetent patients, and 6 to 12 months or more for immunocompromised patients and CNS disease.
• Monitor for TMP-SMX toxicity (hyperkalaemia, raised creatinine, cytopenias, rash), and for linezolid toxicity with long courses.
• Sulfonamide allergy needs specialist advice about desensitization or alternatives (amikacin, imipenem, linezolid, minocycline, ceftriaxone for susceptible isolates).

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Resistance varies by species, so always request susceptibility testing.
• N. farcinica is often resistant to third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones.
• N. nova is typically susceptible to ampicillin and macrolides, whereas N. brasiliensis is often susceptible to amoxicillin-clavulanate.
• Sulfonamide resistance is uncommon but increasing.
• Linezolid and amikacin are active against nearly all isolates.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Wear gloves and protective clothing during soil work in at-risk patients, and clean wounds promptly.
• TMP-SMX prophylaxis given to transplant and HIV patients for Pneumocystis may lower the risk, although breakthrough infection occurs.
• Reduce corticosteroid exposure where possible.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: Branching beaded Gram-positive rods that are weakly acid-fast: Nocardia.
Always image the brain in pulmonary or disseminated nocardiosis.
Ask the laboratory to hold cultures for 2 weeks.
TMP-SMX is the backbone of treatment, and linezolid and imipenem are important partners in severe disease.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Local transplant and infectious diseases guidance on nocardiosis
Specialist reference laboratory susceptibility guidance

organisms.name: Clostridium perfringens
organisms.morphology: Large Gram-positive anaerobic bacilli ('boxcar' shape), non-motile
organisms.tagline: Toxin-producing anaerobe behind gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) and one of the commonest causes of food-borne diarrhoea after reheated meat dishes.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Large, rectangular ('boxcar') Gram-positive bacilli; anaerobic but relatively aerotolerant, and non-motile.
• Spores are rarely seen in tissue or on culture.
• Double zone of haemolysis on blood agar: an inner zone of complete haemolysis (theta toxin) and an outer zone of partial haemolysis (alpha toxin).
• Nagler reaction: lecithinase activity on egg yolk agar, blocked by specific antitoxin; reverse CAMP test positive.
• Ferments many sugars and produces large amounts of gas.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Alpha toxin (lecithinase, phospholipase C) lyses cell membranes, causing myonecrosis, haemolysis and vascular damage; it is the main virulence factor in gas gangrene.
• Theta toxin (perfringolysin O) is a pore-forming toxin that adds to tissue destruction and impairs white cell function.
• Enterotoxin (CPE) binds claudins in the gut, damages tight junctions and causes food poisoning.
• Beta toxin causes necrotizing enteritis (type C strains).
• Rapid growth and gas production separate tissue planes and spread infection quickly.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Widely found in soil, dust and the intestinal tract of humans and animals.
• Gas gangrene follows traumatic or surgical wounds with devitalized tissue and low oxygen, and it is also seen after injections and in intestinal ischaemia or cancer.
• Food poisoning: among the commonest bacterial food-borne illnesses, linked to large batches of meat, poultry and gravies cooked, cooled slowly and reheated, so that spores germinate and multiply.
• Spontaneous gas gangrene without trauma is associated with colon cancer and neutropenia.
• Pigbel is seen mainly in Papua New Guinea in people with low protein intake after pig feasts.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Gas gangrene: sudden severe pain out of proportion to the findings, swelling, tense skin, dusky or bronze discolouration, bullae with serosanguinous fluid, crepitus, foul-smelling discharge, fever, tachycardia and rapid shock.
• Marked haemolysis, jaundice, acute kidney injury and disseminated intravascular coagulation in severe cases.
• Food poisoning: watery diarrhoea and cramps 8 to 16 hours after eating contaminated food; fever and vomiting are uncommon; resolves within 24 hours.
• Necrotizing enteritis: abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea and bowel necrosis.
• Clostridial bacteraemia is rare but can cause fulminant intravascular haemolysis.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Gas gangrene is a clinical emergency: do not wait for laboratory results.
• Gram stain of wound fluid shows large Gram-positive bacilli with few or no neutrophils.
• Imaging (X-ray or CT) can show gas in tissue, but gas can also come from other organisms.
• Anaerobic culture of tissue, fluid and blood; identify with MALDI-TOF.
• Food poisoning: detect enterotoxin in stool or quantify the organism in stool and food in an outbreak; routine stool culture is not helpful.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Urgent surgical exploration and wide debridement of all necrotic tissue, with amputation when needed, is the cornerstone of gas gangrene treatment.
• Penicillin G combined with clindamycin (clindamycin suppresses toxin production) is the classic regimen.
• Add broad-spectrum cover for mixed infection, such as a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam, until cultures are available.
• Intensive care support for shock, kidney failure and coagulopathy; hyperbaric oxygen is sometimes used as an adjunct, but its benefit is unproven and it must not delay surgery.
• Food poisoning: supportive care with oral rehydration; antibiotics are not needed.
• Necrotizing enteritis: bowel rest, antibiotics, supportive care, and surgery for perforation or necrosis.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Generally susceptible to penicillin, metronidazole and carbapenems.
• Some isolates resist clindamycin, tetracycline and macrolides, and clindamycin should not be the sole drug.
• Resistance is not a major issue, but susceptibility testing is helpful in severe or unusual infection.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Prompt wound cleaning and debridement, and removal of foreign material and dead tissue.
• Surgical prophylaxis for relevant procedures.
• Food safety: cook meat thoroughly, cool leftovers quickly, store food below 5 degrees Celsius or above 60 degrees Celsius, and reheat to at least 74 degrees Celsius.
• Pigbel can be prevented with type C toxoid vaccination in endemic areas.
• There is no routine vaccine for gas gangrene.

pearls: Severe wound pain out of proportion to the findings with gas in the tissue is clostridial gas gangrene until proven otherwise.
Boxcar-shaped Gram-positive rods with few white cells in a wound smear: C. perfringens.
Treat surgically first and add penicillin plus clindamycin; do not delay surgery for hyperbaric oxygen.
Reheated meat dishes are the classic source of C. perfringens food poisoning.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Stevens DL et al. IDSA guideline for skin and soft tissue infections. Clin Infect Dis 2014
CDC guidance on Clostridium perfringens food safety

organisms.name: Clostridium botulinum
organisms.tagline: Soil anaerobe producing botulinum neurotoxin, the most potent known toxin, which causes descending flaccid paralysis; food-borne, infant, wound and inhalational forms exist.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Large Gram-positive, strictly anaerobic, spore-forming bacilli with oval subterminal spores.
• Spores are heat-resistant and survive in soil, sediments and many foods; the toxin itself is destroyed by boiling for 10 minutes.
• Eight toxin types (A to G, plus others); types A, B, E and F cause most human disease.
• Grows in low-acid, low-oxygen conditions (pH above 4.6), such as home-canned vegetables and fermented fish.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Botulinum neurotoxin is a zinc metalloprotease made up of a heavy chain (binding and entry) and a light chain.
• The light chain cleaves SNARE proteins (SNAP-25, synaptobrevin or syntaxin, depending on type), which prevents release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction and at autonomic synapses.
• The result is flaccid paralysis; the effect lasts until new nerve terminals are formed, which takes weeks to months.
• The toxin is encoded on phages or plasmids in some types; the disease is toxin-mediated, with no tissue invasion in the food-borne form.
• A tiny amount (nanograms) is lethal, which makes it a bioterrorism concern.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Food-borne: improperly home-canned or preserved foods (vegetables, fish, fermented foods); type E is linked to fish and marine mammals, especially in Alaska.
• Infant botulism: the most common form in the United States; ingestion of spores that colonize the gut of infants under 1 year; linked to honey and to soil or dust.
• Wound botulism: injection drug use (especially black tar heroin) and traumatic wounds.
• Inhalational and iatrogenic (cosmetic and therapeutic toxin overdose) forms are rare.
• Not transmitted between people; any suspected case is a public health emergency.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Symmetrical descending flaccid paralysis with a clear mind and no fever.
• Cranial nerves first: diplopia, ptosis, blurred vision, dilated and poorly reactive pupils, dysphagia, dysarthria and facial weakness, then limb weakness and respiratory failure.
• Autonomic signs: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention and postural hypotension.
• Food-borne: nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain may precede the neurological signs by 12 to 36 hours.
• Infant botulism: constipation, weak cry, poor feeding, drooling, hypotonia ('floppy baby') and loss of head control, which can progress to respiratory failure.
• Differential diagnosis: Guillain-Barre syndrome (ascending, with raised CSF protein and sensory signs), myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome and stroke.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
