• Diagnosis is clinical, and treatment should not wait for laboratory confirmation.
• Contact public health authorities immediately: antitoxin is released through them in many countries.
• Toxin detection in serum, stool, gastric contents or suspected food (mouse bioassay or newer immunoassay and mass spectrometry methods); culture of stool or wound material.
• Infants: stool culture and toxin assay.
• Electromyography shows a characteristic incremental response at high-rate stimulation, with small motor unit potentials.
• CSF is normal, and a Tensilon test is negative or equivocal.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Early botulinum antitoxin is the specific treatment: heptavalent equine antitoxin (BAT) for adults and children, and human-derived botulism immune globulin (BabyBIG) for infant botulism.
• Antitoxin halts progression by neutralizing free toxin, but does not reverse existing paralysis, so give it as early as possible.
• Supportive care is critical: monitor vital capacity, secure the airway and give mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, which may last weeks.
• Wound botulism: debridement of the wound plus antitoxin and penicillin G or another suitable antibiotic.
• Infant botulism: antibiotics are not routinely used; avoid aminoglycosides and some other drugs, which can worsen neuromuscular blockade.
• Recovery takes weeks to months as new nerve terminals grow.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Antibiotic resistance is not a clinical issue.
• Antibiotics play only a limited role: they do not neutralize toxin, and are used mainly for wound botulism.
• Aminoglycosides and clindamycin can worsen neuromuscular blockade and should be avoided.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Follow safe home canning methods (use a pressure canner for low-acid foods), and boil home-canned food for at least 10 minutes before eating.
• Never give honey to infants under 12 months.
• Discard bulging cans and food with an off smell or appearance, and do not taste suspect food.
• Avoid injection drug use, and seek wound care promptly.
• Public health tracing of contaminated food sources; botulinum toxin is a category A bioterrorism agent.
• A botulinum toxoid vaccine is only for selected high-risk laboratory workers, and is not routinely available.

pearls: Descending symmetric flaccid paralysis with a clear mind and no fever: botulism.
Infant botulism: constipation and a floppy baby, and no honey under 12 months.
Give antitoxin on clinical suspicion; it does not reverse existing paralysis.
Guillain-Barre is ascending with sensory signs and raised CSF protein; botulism is descending with normal CSF.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC clinical guidance on botulism
WHO fact sheet on botulism

organisms.name: Streptococcus agalactiae
organisms.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in chains (Group B Streptococcus)
organisms.tagline: Leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, acquired from the mother's genital tract; also causes invasive infection in pregnant women, older adults and people with diabetes.
diseases: Early-onset neonatal sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis
Maternal chorioamnionitis, endometritis and urinary tract infection
Adult bacteraemia, skin and soft tissue infection and diabetic foot infection

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive cocci in short chains; facultative anaerobe and catalase-negative.
• Narrow zone of beta-haemolysis on blood agar, Lancefield group B antigen.
• Hippurate hydrolysis positive, bacitracin-resistant and CAMP test positive (it enhances haemolysis by S. aureus beta-lysin).
• Ten capsular serotypes (Ia, Ib and II to IX), with serotype III causing most late-onset meningitis.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Sialic-acid-rich polysaccharide capsule inhibits phagocytosis and complement deposition.
• Beta-haemolysin/cytolysin damages epithelial and endothelial cells and crosses the lung and blood-brain barriers.
• C5a peptidase cleaves complement C5a, which reduces neutrophil recruitment.
• CAMP factor is a pore-forming protein; surface proteins mediate adhesion and invasion.
• Hyaluronidase and other factors aid tissue spread.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Colonizes the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tract, with about 10 to 30% of pregnant women carrying it.
• Early-onset disease (birth to 6 days) follows vertical transmission during delivery or after membrane rupture; late-onset disease (7 to 89 days) comes from maternal or environmental sources.
• Risk factors for early-onset disease: preterm birth, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever in labour, GBS bacteriuria, and a previous affected infant.
• Adult invasive disease is rising, particularly in people over 65, and those with diabetes, obesity, cirrhosis, cancer or neurological disease.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Early-onset neonatal disease: respiratory distress, apnoea, sepsis and shock in the first hours or days of life; pneumonia and meningitis are common.
• Late-onset neonatal disease: bacteraemia with meningitis, fever, irritability and poor feeding, and sometimes bone, joint or skin involvement.
• Meningitis can cause long-term neurological sequelae.
• Pregnant women: asymptomatic bacteriuria, urinary tract infection, chorioamnionitis and endometritis.
• Adults: cellulitis, diabetic foot infection, bacteraemia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, endocarditis and urinary tract infection.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Blood culture in neonates with suspected sepsis, and lumbar puncture when meningitis is possible; culture of CSF.
• Maternal screening with a rectovaginal swab culture or nucleic acid amplification test at 36 to 37 weeks of gestation (and sooner if preterm labour).
• Test urine in pregnancy: any GBS bacteriuria counts as colonization and needs intrapartum prophylaxis.
• In adults, culture blood, tissue or joint fluid, and search for a source, with echocardiography if bacteraemic.
• GBS PCR is available for rapid testing at the time of labour in some settings.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Neonatal sepsis or meningitis: start empirical ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside (or a third-generation cephalosporin in some settings), and narrow to penicillin G or ampicillin when GBS is identified.
• Adults: penicillin G or ampicillin is the drug of choice; a cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone or cefazolin is an alternative.
• Penicillin allergy: use cefazolin if the reaction is low risk; use vancomycin or clindamycin (if the isolate is susceptible) for high-risk allergy.
• Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is given to colonized women: intravenous penicillin G or ampicillin at least 4 hours before delivery, which prevents most early-onset disease.
• Duration depends on the site: bacteraemia 10 days, meningitis 14 days or longer, and bone and joint infection 4 to 6 weeks.
• Endocarditis and osteomyelitis need extended therapy and specialist review.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• All isolates remain susceptible to penicillin, although reduced penicillin susceptibility has been reported rarely.
• Resistance to erythromycin and clindamycin is common and rising (erm and mef genes), which matters for penicillin-allergic women.
• Test clindamycin susceptibility with a D-test for inducible resistance in penicillin-allergic women.
• Fluoroquinolone resistance is increasingly reported.
• Vancomycin remains active.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Universal screening of pregnant women at 36 to 37 weeks, with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for carriers and for women with risk factors, has greatly reduced early-onset disease.
• Prophylaxis does not prevent late-onset disease.
• Newborns of colonized or high-risk mothers are observed or evaluated according to guidelines.
• Maternal vaccines against GBS capsular polysaccharides are in development, but none is licensed yet.
• Good diabetic foot care and skin care help prevent adult infection.

pearls: CAMP-positive, hippurate-positive, bacitracin-resistant beta-haemolytic streptococci are group B.
Penicillin or ampicillin at least 4 hours before delivery prevents most early-onset GBS disease.
GBS is the commonest cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis in many countries, and Listeria is the other classic cause to cover with ampicillin.
Test clindamycin susceptibility before using it in penicillin-allergic women.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
ACOG Committee Opinion on prevention of group B streptococcal early-onset disease in newborns
CDC guidance on group B streptococcus

organisms.name: Yersinia pestis
organisms.tagline: Flea-borne zoonotic pathogen causing plague: bubonic, septicaemic and highly contagious pneumonic disease, with rapid death if treatment is delayed.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Small Gram-negative coccobacilli; facultative anaerobe, non-motile and non-lactose fermenting.
• Bipolar staining with Wayson or Giemsa stain gives a 'safety-pin' appearance.
• Grows slowly on blood agar and MacConkey agar, with optimal growth at 28 degrees Celsius; colonies look like 'fried eggs' or 'hammered copper' after 48 hours.
• Oxidase-negative and urease-negative (Y. pseudotuberculosis is urease-positive).
• A biosafety level 3 organism and a category A bioterrorism agent.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• The type III secretion system injects Yersinia outer proteins (Yops) that block phagocytosis and suppress inflammation; V antigen (LcrV) and W antigen are virulence-associated.
• F1 capsule antigen is antiphagocytic and is also the target of rapid diagnostic tests and some vaccines.
• Pla (plasminogen activator) protease promotes spread from the flea bite site to lymph nodes and the lungs.
• Yersiniabactin siderophore captures iron, and the pH 6 antigen aids survival in macrophages.
• In fleas, biofilm blocks the proventriculus, so the hungry flea regurgitates bacteria into bite sites; murine toxin helps survival in the flea gut.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Maintained in wild rodents and their fleas; humans are accidental hosts, infected by flea bites (Xenopsylla cheopis), handling infected animals, or inhaling droplets from a person or animal with pneumonic disease.
• Three historic pandemics, including the Black Death; plague is still present in Madagascar, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Peru and the south-western United States.
• Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person by respiratory droplets, and can cause outbreaks.
• Cats and dogs can bring infected fleas or become sources of pneumonic spread.
• Plague is a notifiable disease under international health regulations.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Incubation 2 to 8 days for bubonic plague, shorter for pneumonic disease (1 to 4 days).
• Bubonic: sudden fever, chills and a very painful, swollen regional lymph node (bubo) in the groin, axilla or neck, with surrounding oedema.
• Septicaemic: shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpura and gangrene of fingers and toes ('Black Death'), sometimes without a bubo.
• Pneumonic: rapid, severe pneumonia with cough, haemoptysis and respiratory failure; almost always fatal if untreated.
• Meningitis can follow bacteraemia.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Suspect plague in a febrile patient with a painful bubo and exposure to rodents, fleas or endemic areas.
• Notify the laboratory and public health at once: handle specimens with biosafety precautions.
• Gram, Giemsa or Wayson stain of bubo aspirate, sputum or blood; culture of blood, aspirate or sputum.
• Rapid F1 antigen dipstick, PCR and direct fluorescent antibody tests provide faster confirmation.
• Start treatment on clinical suspicion: do not wait for results.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Start antibiotics immediately; mortality rises sharply with delay (pneumonic plague should be treated within 24 hours of symptoms).
• Streptomycin or gentamicin is first-line; doxycycline, ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin are alternatives, and fluoroquinolones or doxycycline are commonly used in outbreaks.
• Meningitis: chloramphenicol, because of good CSF penetration.
• Pneumonic plague: droplet precautions until at least 48 hours of effective therapy, and isolation of patients.
• Post-exposure prophylaxis for close contacts of pneumonic cases: doxycycline or ciprofloxacin for 7 days.
• Supportive care in intensive care for shock and respiratory failure.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Natural resistance is rare, and most strains are susceptible to the usual drugs.
• A multidrug-resistant strain with a plasmid (IncA/C) has been found in Madagascar, with resistance to streptomycin, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol and others.
• Susceptibility testing should be done by a reference laboratory.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Flea and rodent control, and keeping homes and food stores rodent-proof.
• Use insect repellent and avoid handling sick or dead animals in endemic areas; treat pets for fleas.
• Protective equipment and surveillance for people at occupational risk.
• Early detection and isolation of pneumonic plague cases and prophylaxis for contacts.
• A licensed vaccine is not widely available; killed whole-cell vaccines are no longer routine.

pearls: A painful swollen lymph node with fever after rodent or flea exposure is plague until proven otherwise.
Bipolar 'safety-pin' staining Gram-negative coccobacilli: Yersinia pestis.
Treat suspected pneumonic plague within 24 hours, with droplet isolation.
Streptomycin and gentamicin are the classic first-line agents.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
CDC clinical guidance on plague
WHO guidance on plague management and prevention

organisms.name: Brucella species
organisms.morphology: Small Gram-negative coccobacilli, aerobic, non-motile, facultative intracellular
organisms.tagline: Zoonotic pathogen from livestock causing undulant fever with relapses, spondylitis and sacroiliitis, and endocarditis; contracted from unpasteurised dairy or occupational exposure.
diseases: Acute and undulant brucellosis (fever with sweats)

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Small Gram-negative coccobacilli; strictly aerobic (some species need extra CO2), non-motile and non-spore-forming.
• Oxidase-positive, catalase-positive and urease-positive; slow growth on blood or chocolate agar.
• Four species cause most human disease: B. melitensis (goats and sheep), B. abortus (cattle), B. suis (pigs) and B. canis (dogs); B. melitensis is the most virulent.
• Facultative intracellular organism that survives in macrophages.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Smooth lipopolysaccharide (LPS) with low endotoxin activity, so that the bacteria evade early immune detection.
• Type IV secretion system (VirB) delivers effectors that create a replicative vacuole, which does not fuse with lysosomes.
• Survives and multiplies inside macrophages, so it can persist in the reticuloendothelial system (liver, spleen, bone marrow).
• Cell-mediated immunity (Th1 and interferon-gamma) controls infection, which explains relapses and chronic disease.
• Erythritol in animal placentas explains the tropism for the reproductive tract in animals.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Transmitted by unpasteurised milk and soft cheese, contact with infected animal tissues, aerosols and accidental inoculation.
• Occupational risk: farmers, veterinarians, abattoir workers and laboratory staff (brucellosis is among the commonest laboratory-acquired infections).
• Endemic in the Mediterranean, the Middle East, Central Asia, parts of Africa and Latin America; many countries have controlled it through animal vaccination and pasteurisation.
• Person-to-person spread is very rare (breastfeeding, sexual contact, transplantation).
• Notifiable in many countries, and the organism is a potential bioterrorism agent.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Incubation 1 to 4 weeks, sometimes months.
• Fever that may be undulant (waxing and waning), drenching sweats with a characteristic odour, malaise, weight loss, headache and arthralgia.
• Osteoarticular disease is the commonest complication: sacroiliitis, spondylitis, large-joint arthritis.
• Epididymo-orchitis in men; hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy.
• Endocarditis (mainly aortic valve) carries the highest mortality; neurobrucellosis includes meningoencephalitis.
• Brucellosis in pregnancy can cause miscarriage; relapses occur in about 10% of cases after treatment.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Take an exposure history: unpasteurised dairy, animal contact, travel to endemic areas.
• Blood cultures positive in many cases, especially early; warn the laboratory because of biosafety risk, and cultures may need up to 4 weeks, although modern systems usually detect growth in 5 to 7 days.
• Serology: standard agglutination test with titre of 1:160 or more, or a four-fold rise, and Rose Bengal screening; the 2-mercaptoethanol test and Coombs help in chronic cases.
• Bone marrow culture is more sensitive; PCR is useful in selected cases.
• Imaging (X-ray, MRI) of the spine and sacroiliac joints; echocardiography when endocarditis is suspected.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Combination therapy for at least 6 weeks, because single drugs have high relapse rates.
• Doxycycline plus rifampicin for 6 weeks, or doxycycline for 6 weeks with an aminoglycoside (streptomycin or gentamicin) for the first 2 to 3 weeks, which is more effective for focal disease.
• Spondylitis, neurobrucellosis and endocarditis need longer courses (3 to 6 months or more) and specialist advice; neurobrucellosis regimens include ceftriaxone for CNS penetration.
• Endocarditis: antibiotics plus surgical valve replacement in most cases.
• Children under 8: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus rifampicin or an aminoglycoside; pregnancy: rifampicin with or without trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, with specialist advice.
• Follow patients for at least a year for relapse.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Resistance to the main drugs is rare.
• Relapse after treatment is usually due to short courses, poor adherence or monotherapy, and not to resistance.
• Rifampicin resistance has been reported in some regions, which is of concern where tuberculosis is also endemic.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Pasteurise milk and avoid unpasteurised dairy, particularly soft cheese.
• Livestock vaccination and test-and-slaughter programmes control animal disease.
• Wear gloves, masks and protective clothing when handling animal birth products, and follow biosafety rules in the laboratory.
• Post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk laboratory exposures with doxycycline plus rifampicin for 3 weeks.
• No licensed human vaccine.

pearls: Fever with drenching sweats, sacroiliitis and unpasteurised cheese or livestock contact: brucellosis.
Always use combination therapy, because monotherapy has high relapse rates.
Warn the laboratory before sending blood cultures.
Endocarditis is the main cause of death in brucellosis.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
WHO guidance on brucellosis in humans and animals
CDC clinical guidance on brucellosis

organisms.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
organisms.morphology: Motile Gram-negative bacilli with bipolar staining, aerobic
organisms.tagline: Soil and water bacterium causing melioidosis, a severe infection mostly in people with diabetes across South-East Asia and northern Australia, with a wide range from pneumonia to abscesses and fatal sepsis.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Motile Gram-negative bacilli that show bipolar ('safety-pin') staining; aerobic non-fermenter.
• Oxidase-positive; grows on MacConkey agar and, with selective media such as Ashdown agar, forms wrinkled, purple colonies after 2 to 4 days.
• Intrinsically resistant to colistin, polymyxins and gentamicin, which helps selective culture (media with gentamicin and colistin).
• A biosafety level 3 organism, and a recognised bioterrorism agent; easily misidentified by some automated systems.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Type III and type VI secretion systems enable invasion of host cells and cell-to-cell spread (multinucleated giant cell formation).
• Capsular polysaccharide is antiphagocytic, and BimA drives actin-based motility.
• Survives and multiplies inside macrophages and other cells, so it can remain latent for years.
• Lipopolysaccharide and secreted factors contribute to sepsis, and biofilm formation protects against antibiotics.
• Host factors are crucial: diabetes and other conditions impair neutrophil and macrophage function.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Lives in soil and surface water in tropical regions: endemic in South-East Asia (especially north-east Thailand), northern Australia, and increasingly recognised in South Asia, parts of Africa, South America and the Caribbean.
• Infection follows skin inoculation, inhalation or ingestion, and most cases occur in the rainy season, after heavy rain, floods or cyclones.
• Diabetes mellitus is the most important risk factor; others include excess alcohol, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease, thalassaemia and immunosuppression.
• Person-to-person spread is rare; infection after laboratory exposure and in travellers occurs.
• Incubation is usually 1 to 21 days, but latent disease can reactivate after years.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Highly variable ('the great mimicker'): from localised skin infection to fulminant sepsis.
• Pneumonia is the commonest presentation, either acute with rapid progression, or chronic and mimicking tuberculosis with upper-lobe cavities.
• Bacteraemia and septic shock with multiple abscesses, particularly in the liver, spleen, prostate and kidneys.
• Skin: pustules, ulcers and abscesses; neurological forms include brainstem encephalomyelitis; osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.
• Parotid abscess in Thai children is characteristic.
• Mortality remains high in septicaemic disease, even with treatment.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Consider melioidosis in any febrile patient with diabetes or other risk factors who lives in or has travelled to an endemic area, including remote exposure.
• Culture of blood, sputum, throat swab, rectal swab, urine or pus on selective media; alert the laboratory to the suspicion.
• Rapid immunofluorescence, latex agglutination and PCR on isolates or clinical samples can speed up diagnosis.
• Serology is unreliable in endemic areas because of high background antibody.
• CT or ultrasound to look for deep abscesses in the liver, spleen, prostate and kidneys.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Intensive phase with intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem for at least 10 to 14 days, and longer (4 to 8 weeks) for deep-seated infection, osteomyelitis and neurological disease; meropenem is preferred for severe disease and intensive care.
• Eradication phase: oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for at least 3 to 6 months (doxycycline or amoxicillin-clavulanate if intolerant), to prevent relapse.
• Drain abscesses when feasible, and control blood sugar.
• Add trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in neurological and prostatic disease because of better tissue penetration.
• Poor adherence to eradication therapy is the commonest cause of relapse.
• Follow for at least a year after treatment.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsic resistance to penicillin, ampicillin, first- and second-generation cephalosporins, gentamicin and other aminoglycosides, and polymyxins.
• Acquired ceftazidime resistance (penA mutations) and rare resistance to meropenem or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole have been reported.
• Efflux pumps (such as AmrAB-OprA) and beta-lactamases contribute to resistance.
• Susceptibility testing is important in relapse and treatment failure.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• In endemic areas, avoid contact with soil and muddy water during the rainy season, and wear boots and gloves for agriculture.
• People with diabetes, kidney disease or other risk factors should cover open wounds and avoid exposure to soil and surface water.
• Drink boiled or bottled water.
• Post-exposure prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for high-risk exposures (for example laboratory exposure).
• No licensed vaccine is available.

pearls: Pneumonia, abscesses and sepsis in a diabetic person from South-East Asia or northern Australia: think melioidosis.
Oxidase-positive Gram-negative bacilli resistant to gentamicin and colistin with safety-pin staining suggest B. pseudomallei.
Treatment has two phases: IV ceftazidime or meropenem, then 3 to 6 months of oral TMP-SMX.
Always warn the laboratory: it is a biosafety level 3 organism.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Currie BJ. Melioidosis: evolving concepts in epidemiology, pathogenesis and treatment. Semin Respir Crit Care Med 2015
Lipsitz R et al. Workshop on treatment of and postexposure prophylaxis for Burkholderia pseudomallei and B. mallei infection. Emerg Infect Dis 2012

organisms.name: Staphylococcus epidermidis
organisms.tagline: Skin commensal and the leading cause of infections on catheters and prosthetic devices, through biofilm formation; also the commonest blood culture contaminant.
diseases: CSF shunt and other neurosurgical device infection
Late-onset neonatal sepsis in preterm infants

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase-positive and coagulase-negative.
• Non-haemolytic, white colonies on blood agar; does not ferment mannitol.
• Novobiocin-sensitive, which separates it from S. saprophyticus (novobiocin-resistant, a cause of urinary infection in young women).
• Identified by MALDI-TOF or other automated systems.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Biofilm formation is the central factor: polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (encoded by the ica operon), Aap and Embp proteins bind to plastic and host proteins on devices.
• Biofilm protects bacteria from phagocytes and antibiotics, and makes device infection hard to cure without removing the device.
• Phenol-soluble modulins, and the agr quorum-sensing system, regulate virulence and dispersal.
• Few classic toxins, so it acts as an opportunistic pathogen of low virulence.
• Frequently carries mecA on the SCCmec cassette, giving methicillin resistance.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Dominant part of normal skin flora, found on all humans.
• The commonest cause of nosocomial bloodstream infection and device-related infection.
• Risk factors: central venous catheters, prosthetic valves and joints, shunts, pacemakers, dialysis catheters, prematurity and immunosuppression.
• Most positive blood cultures are contaminants: a single positive bottle from a patient without a device usually reflects skin contamination.
• Hospital isolates are mostly methicillin-resistant.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Catheter-related bloodstream infection: low-grade fever, with local signs at the line site sometimes absent.
• Prosthetic valve endocarditis, especially early (within a year of surgery); native valve endocarditis is rare.
• Prosthetic joint infection: pain, loosening, swelling and sometimes a sinus tract; often indolent.
• CSF shunt infection: headache, shunt malfunction or low-grade fever.
• Neonatal late-onset sepsis: apnoea, temperature instability and poor feeding in preterm infants with lines.
• Disease tends to be subacute, and rarely causes septic shock.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Interpret the clinical context: the same species and antibiogram in two or more separate blood culture sets (or in a blood culture and a catheter tip) supports true infection.
• A single positive culture in a patient without a device is usually a contaminant.
• Catheter tip culture (more than 15 colonies by roll-plate) or paired quantitative cultures, and differential time to positivity.
• Echocardiography for suspected endocarditis; synovial fluid or intra-operative tissue cultures for joint infection.
• Take multiple deep tissue samples when possible, because sonication of explanted devices increases yield.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Remove or replace the infected device whenever possible: antibiotics alone often fail because of biofilm.
• Methicillin-resistant strains (most isolates): vancomycin is the usual first choice; daptomycin or linezolid are alternatives.
• Methicillin-susceptible strains: an anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam such as cefazolin, nafcillin or oxacillin.
• Rifampin is added for prosthetic material infection because it penetrates biofilm, but never alone, and only after bacteraemia has cleared, because resistance emerges quickly.
• Prosthetic joint infection needs surgery (debridement with implant retention, or one- or two-stage revision) and prolonged antibiotics.
• Catheter-related infection without a retained device may be treated with antibiotic lock therapy in selected cases.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Methicillin resistance (mecA) is found in most hospital isolates, so beta-lactams other than newer anti-MRSA cephalosporins fail.
• Many strains are also resistant to macrolides, clindamycin, gentamicin and fluoroquinolones.
• Rifampin resistance develops rapidly when used alone.
• Linezolid resistance (cfr gene, and 23S rRNA mutations) and reduced vancomycin susceptibility are reported.
• Always request susceptibility results before choosing therapy.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Strict aseptic technique and maximal barrier precautions when inserting central lines.
• Chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, daily review of the need for lines and early removal.
• Antibiotic prophylaxis before prosthetic joint or cardiac surgery.
• Hand hygiene, and careful line and catheter care bundles.
• Antibiotic lock solutions in selected long-term catheter patients.

pearls: Coagulase-negative staphylococcus in a single blood culture bottle is usually a contaminant.
Novobiocin-sensitive: S. epidermidis; novobiocin-resistant: S. saprophyticus.
Biofilm means the device usually has to come out.
Rifampin is never used as monotherapy.
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases, 9th edition
Mermel LA et al. IDSA guidelines for catheter-related bloodstream infection. Clin Infect Dis 2009
Osmon DR et al. IDSA guidelines for prosthetic joint infection. Clin Infect Dis 2013

organisms.name: Proteus mirabilis
organisms.tagline: Urease-producing Enterobacterales that causes catheter-associated urinary infection and struvite (infection) stones, with swarming motility on culture plates.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Gram-negative, motile bacilli; facultative anaerobe.
• Swarming: waves of growth across blood agar, which can hide other colonies.
• Non-lactose fermenter (colourless colonies on MacConkey), and produces H2S (black centres on XLD).
• Strongly urease-positive, indole-negative; P. vulgaris is indole-positive.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, which raises urine pH and causes magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and calcium phosphate crystals to precipitate.
• Peritrichous flagella and swarming differentiation aid ascent of the urinary tract.
• MR/P fimbriae adhere to uroepithelium; haemolysin and IgA protease damage tissue and evade immunity.
• Biofilm and crystalline deposits on catheters protect bacteria and block drainage.
• Lipopolysaccharide endotoxin contributes to sepsis.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Lives in the human gut and the environment, and is a common urinary pathogen.
• The commonest cause of complicated urinary infection after E. coli and Klebsiella, especially in long-term catheterised patients.
• Risk factors: indwelling catheters, urinary tract abnormalities, stones, neurogenic bladder, diabetes, older age and long-term care.
• Community-onset infection occurs in people with structural abnormalities.
• ESBL-producing and fluoroquinolone-resistant strains are increasing.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Cystitis and pyelonephritis with fever, dysuria and flank pain.
• Alkaline urine (pH above 7.5), sometimes with a fishy or ammoniacal smell.
• Struvite stones that grow rapidly to fill the renal pelvis (staghorn calculi) and cause recurrent infection, obstruction and loss of kidney function.
• Catheter encrustation and blockage; bacteraemia and urosepsis in older or immunocompromised patients.
• Wound, ear (chronic otitis media) and, rarely, neonatal infection.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• Urine culture with swarming and urease positivity, and susceptibility testing.
• Urinalysis shows alkaline pH and may show struvite crystals (coffin-lid shaped).
• CT or ultrasound of the kidneys to look for stones and obstruction in recurrent infection.
• Blood cultures if the patient has fever or signs of sepsis.
• Differentiate colonisation (asymptomatic catheter bacteriuria) from infection.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Treat according to susceptibility: ampicillin or amoxicillin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones are often active.
• Pyelonephritis and urosepsis: ceftriaxone or another suitable intravenous agent, with a carbapenem for ESBL producers.
• Struvite stones need urological removal, because antibiotics alone cannot sterilise them; consider urease inhibitors only in selected cases.
• Replace or remove an infected catheter, and relieve obstruction.
• Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients, except in pregnancy and before urological procedures.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Intrinsically resistant to nitrofurantoin, tetracyclines and tigecycline, and polymyxins (colistin).
• Reduced susceptibility to imipenem compared with other carbapenems.
• Acquired resistance: ESBLs, plasmid AmpC and carbapenemases, plus fluoroquinolone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance.
• Choose antibiotics by local resistance patterns and culture results.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Avoid unnecessary urinary catheters, and remove them as early as possible.
• Aseptic catheter care, closed drainage systems, and adequate hydration.
• Remove stones and correct urological abnormalities.
• Do not screen or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.
• No vaccine is available.

pearls: Alkaline urine, swarming and urease-positive: Proteus.
Staghorn calculi mean struvite stones from urease-producing bacteria, so infection persists until the stone is removed.
Nitrofurantoin does not work against Proteus.
Indole-positive: P. vulgaris; indole-negative: P. mirabilis.

organisms.name: Chlamydia pneumoniae
organisms.morphology: Obligate intracellular bacterium (elementary and reticulate bodies)
organisms.tagline: Common cause of mild community-acquired respiratory infection (atypical pneumonia, bronchitis, pharyngitis and sinusitis), spread person to person; treated with doxycycline, a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.

sections.title: Microbiology
sections.text:
• Obligate intracellular bacterium; cannot grow on routine media, and has no peptidoglycan layer detectable by Gram stain.
• Life cycle: infectious elementary body enters the cell, converts into a reticulate body that replicates in an inclusion, and then back to elementary bodies.
• Unlike C. trachomatis, the inclusions do not stain with iodine (no glycogen), and the elementary body is pear-shaped on electron microscopy.
• Only one serovar (TWAR strain); grows poorly in cell culture, so culture is not used routinely.

sections.title: Virulence Factors
sections.text:
• Attaches to and invades respiratory epithelial cells and macrophages.
• Type III secretion system effectors modify host cell function and block lysosomal fusion.
• Persistent forms can survive in cells, leading to chronic or repeated infection.
• The chlamydial heat shock protein 60 and lipopolysaccharide drive inflammation.
• Ciliostasis and epithelial damage impair clearance.

sections.title: Epidemiology
sections.text:
• Humans are the only reservoir; spread by respiratory droplets, usually with a slow spread through households and institutions.
• Accounts for about 5 to 10% of community-acquired pneumonia and is a cause of bronchitis and sinusitis.
• Infection is common: most adults have antibodies by middle age, and reinfection occurs.
• School-age children, young adults and older people are mostly affected; outbreaks in crowded settings (military, schools, nursing homes).
• Incubation is about 3 to 4 weeks.

sections.title: Clinical Features
sections.text:
• Gradual onset of sore throat or hoarseness, followed by a persistent dry cough lasting weeks, with low-grade fever and malaise.
• Pneumonia is usually mild, and chest X-ray often looks worse than the patient; severe illness is uncommon except in older adults and those with chronic disease.
• Sinusitis and bronchitis; may trigger asthma and COPD exacerbations.
• Extrapulmonary features are less frequent: erythema nodosum, reactive arthritis, Guillain-Barre syndrome and myocarditis have been reported.
• Co-infection with other pathogens such as S. pneumoniae occurs.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text:
• PCR of nasopharyngeal or throat swabs or sputum is the best test, often as part of multiplex respiratory panels.
• Serology with microimmunofluorescence (MIF): acute IgM of 1:16 or more, a four-fold rise in IgG in paired samples, or a single IgG titre of 1:512 or more suggests acute infection; the test is slow and often only retrospective.
• Culture is difficult and not routine.
• Gram stain and routine culture are unhelpful.
• Considered in pneumonia without response to beta-lactam treatment.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text:
• Doxycycline for 10 to 14 days, or a macrolide (azithromycin or clarithromycin), or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin).
• Beta-lactams are ineffective, because the organism lacks a peptidoglycan target and lives inside cells.
• Azithromycin is often preferred for convenience and in pregnancy; doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy and in young children.
• Mild infections may resolve without treatment, though antibiotics speed recovery.
• Treat for longer than for typical bacterial infections, because relapse is possible with short courses.

sections.title: Resistance
sections.text:
• Clinically significant resistance to doxycycline, macrolides or fluoroquinolones has not been established.
• Treatment failures are usually explained by short courses, co-infection or an alternative diagnosis.
• Beta-lactams and aminoglycosides are inactive in practice.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.text:
• Respiratory hygiene, handwashing and avoidance of close contact with infected people.
• Outbreak control measures in institutions.
• No vaccine is available.
• Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for contacts is not recommended.

pearls: Pneumonia that fails to improve on a beta-lactam: think atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella).
Sore throat and hoarseness followed by a prolonged cough suggests C. pneumoniae.
Doxycycline, macrolides and respiratory fluoroquinolones cover atypicals; beta-lactams do not.
The link with atherosclerosis is an association, not proven cause.
